She : "Invariably." He: "And can nothing ever change your determination when you once make up your mind ? " She: "Absolutely nothing." He: "Well, I wouldn't care to marry . woman like that anyhow." Mr DEAR Mum, • -2—For morning wear, silk or viyella shirts, made with three box-pleats down the front, the centre one ornamented with studs or buttons, or another style, somewhat like a Russian blouse, pouched at the waist, and wrapped over to the left side, revealing a small 'stitched taffetas or lace collar and yoke at the neck, are most in vogue. Many of the flannel shirts are ornamented with coarse lace medallions or large botton-holed rings through which silk or lace scarves are pulled. More dressy blouses are fulled or fitting bodices, cut away round the neck and down the centre, to show an under-bodice of lace or embroidery, fur often taking the place of these if it be intended for out- door wear. The pretty little blouses of esprit net, with quaint fichus and frilled elbow sleeves, are only just beginning their successful career, and are likely to have a long life before them. They are very becoming and youthful-looking, nor are the silk and lace slips at all likely to decline in favour, and may be safely recommended as excellent sale investments.
PART IL-CHAPTER IV.

Thera is little new in the way of dress to chronicle, for all the world is busy bargain-hunting ' at the mid-winter sales. Among the things which are selling most briskly at the moment are grey and white felt hats of the Marquise shape, which has a low crown and moderately wide brim, turned up in three places. These hats are generally broadly bound with black, and trimmed with a very full bow of black velvet or panne, and a single large quill, in front. Sometimes a paste buckle is added, and a cluster of violets or pansies is tucked under the brim, while in a few specimens the wide binding is replaced by rows of chenille threaded through holes pierced in the edge of the brim. Cloth toques are being sold off very cheaply, and for immediate wear are not a bad investment, although as a matter of fact it is easy enough to make one at home for a still smaller sum. Half a yard of cloth is more than sufficient for a large toque, and a yard of narrow fur trimming, or the same quantity of heavy guipure or crochet-lace, with a pretty buckle, will be all that is needed, beyond the buckram shape and a bit of silk for Lining, to make a very smart hat Pale blue is a very fashionable colour for these toques, but a goodly number of white, grey, and bright red ones are also to be seen. A red hat is rather too con- spicuous to be worn by everybody, but a girl not much over 20, with dark hair and a clear com- plexion, may safely venture on one, provided that the rest of her costume is subdued in colour— black, steel-grey, or Havana-brown, for instance.

Most of the velvet coats are noted chiefly for their simplicity, the velvet being considered hand. some enough by itself without added decoration, which so often spoils the grace and beauty of its very simplicity. One, plain in cut, with long, gracefully flowing lines, was relieved by a collar and yoke effect in white Irish lace. A narrow band of lace was turned back over the sleeves. A somewhat similar one was trimmed only with finely pleated mousseline de soie bunched at regular intervals down the front of the coat in large choux, ornamented with silver and black buttons. No chou came above the bust line, and from under the last chou fell a full pleating of mousseline to the foot of the garment. Many of these velvet coats have collars and stole-like ends of sable, chinchilla, or ermine, and nearly all are lined with heavy white satin.

The reappearance of the gigot sleeve is fore. shadowed in a lovely dress made of mignonette. green silk muslin over pink satin of a very pale shade. The silk muslin is longitudinally tucked and finished round the edge with horizontal tuck- Ines. The lace that trims the front breadth is bordered with flowers made of silk and chiffon. The sleeves are pronouncedly of the leg-of-mutton shape. A dainty touch is contributed by bands of black velvet brought from the e;de seams of the bodice, crossed in front, and tied at the back after being passed through a large silver buckle. The suds were finished with silver tassels. A wonder- Eul tea-c-iwn of Empire shape is made of rose-pink satin, veiled with an overdress of ecru lace. Quantities of frillings and frou-frous edge the skirt. A short bolero is made of crushed ross-pink satin, and fully trimmed with roses in relief and violets. The sleeves are loose and flowing. This is worn in the morning, and is changed for a race costume of blue striped silk veiled with gauze, trimmed with panne shaded in greenish blue. The toque is large, and carried out in the same colour- ing, shades of greenish blue.

A. LADY one day came upon a poet as he stood absorbed in contemplation before a flock of sheep, and said to him " I feel sure that from the sight of those innocent sheep you are gathering inspira- tion for some gallant pastoral ! " "Oh, dear, no !" replied the poet, "I was only thinking that out of so many sheep there would perhaps be only one leg of mutton done to a turn !" AT a sale of pictures, two amateurs obstinately disputed the possession of a work by a celebrated artist. Each made the biddings against the other. The picture represented an ass. At last one of the gentlemen said, "It's of no use ; I will not yield. The picture once belonged to my uncle, and I will give anything for it." "In that case," said his adversary, "I will not go on. You shall have it, as it is a family portrait."
Your loving, Jumuna.

During the last few years, the squalor of the East. end. of London has been relieved by the throwing open of several small public gardens or recreation grounds veritable oases in the dismal desert of sor- did streets by which they are surrounded. Very pleasant to the wayfarer in these parts in summer time is the unexpected sight Of one of these open spaces, with its well-kept lawns and brilliant flower beds, its green trees with their waving branches and cool shady seats beneath. Truly the money laid out upon these places could hardly have been better spent, and those public-spirited persons who have been the means of bringing it all about deserve more thanks than they are ever likely to receive. To niun- hers of the poor in these regions the sight c.f. the flowers and the cool green must be as refreshing as water to the thirsty, and can scarcely fail to exercise a humanising influence; and certainly hundreds now flock into these gardens and it out their evenings there, watching their children in the playgrounds, or listening to the bands, who, a short while ago. would have spent the same time in public-houses simply because no other place was open to them. In one of these gardens' one afternoon, a young girl was seated, talking to a good-looking young fellow of about five-and-twenty years of age. The girl was Lizzie Collins, niece of the John Collins of whom Dr. L— had spoken to Mr. 'Heiden ; and her companion was James Watson, her sweetheart. The girl's face was sweet and pleasing in expression, and indeed she was known to be one of the prettiest and most attractive maidens in the neighbourhood. But to-day there were tears in her eyes, though her pale cheeks and compressed lips showed she was striving to conceal the feelings of distress the tears betrayed. 'Watson was a carpenter by trade, an was both steady and hard-working ; be had cdurted Lizzie since their childhood, and, till two or three years before, had been encouraged by her father; but recently the latter had forbidden him the house, and the only way the two now had of seeing one an- other was to meet thus occasionally by stealth in the public garden not far from Lizzie 's home. " I tell you I can't stand it no longer, Liz," said Watson. "I'm going away." " But why go away, Jim? That will only make things worse, make us both—certainly make ice— more unhappy than ever," objected Lizzie. "Because I can't stand by and see things go on. I shall do something desperate if I stay; punch Tom Benton's head, or something." "Oh dear !" the girl sighed. "And it used to be so different. I can't make it out at all. Seems rore bad luck all round somehow—for such a long eime." "Yes, ever since your Uncle John came home from abroad, three years ago now." " Hush ! Don't put it on poor Uncle. You know it is not his doing; and he is ill now—so Bl— and lying all alone there at the hospital." "I don't want to say anything against him; I only say it all began when he came back," said Watson doggedly. "Yes, so it did. That's true. It seems strange; almost as if he had brought us bad luck, as you say. An.' I know poor Uncle thinks so hisself, and worries about it. .An' he puts it all down to some horrid gold image he brought back with him. He says it's brought him and all of us bad luck. So many things have gone wrong. The place afire once, and we all nearly burnt to death in our beds. Then father's Unit') down and breakin' his leg andhaving to go to the hospital, and bog= out of work for so long, and our baying to take in that lodger, Tom Benton, and—" "An' he gammoning your father till he wanted you to marry him," Watson growled savagely. "An' all because the fellow seems to have a little money and flashes it about like. Though where he gets it from is more than I can make out. He does precious little work, I know that. And then, too "—and here he lowered his voice—" I'm sure I've seen him, more than once, comiir sneakin' out of Job Patten's. lc ow everybody knows about Job. Ask any police- man about him, an' he'll tell you. He's a fence, that's what he is ; a receiver of stolen goods—only they ain't cotched him trippin' yet." " I don't know," the girl wearily replied, "1 don't know what he is, an' I don't care. Pie told you I don't like him, an' I'll never marry him. But leave the old people to come to you I can't neither —not yet." ," Then I shall go," Watson answered, gloomily. " I can't stand it no longer." Presently they parted, and the girl went sadly back to her home, where she shut herself in her little bedroom and burst into a passionate fit of weeping. In this, she was surprised by be_r mower, who wonder- ingly inquired what it was all sioui. Jim's goin' away," sobbed Lizzie, heartbroken- ly, an' I s'pose I'll never see him any more. He'll forget all about me and like somebody else—you see if he doesn't. And it's all through father and that horrid Tom Benton, the brute ! I hate him ! that I do ; and I'll never marry him. So there." And the flung herself down on the bed and. hid her face in the pillow. " Speakin' o' Benton," said Mrs. Collins, " I wanted to ask yer if ye's seen him. He ain't bin home all night." But Lizzie only stamped with one foot on the floor to signify that she cared nothing what had, be- come of Tom Benton. Just then there was a knock at the street door. Mrs. Collins went to open it, and was greatly surprised to see a strange gentleman. He introduced himself as Arthur Meldon. " I've just come from the hospital where Mr. John Collins is lying ill," he said, " and Dr. L is coming on here directly. I want to have a few Words with you. And is your daugher in? I should like to speak to her, too." " She's in, sir, but I don't know whether she can see you," said the mother, dubiou'gly, remembering her daughter's red eyes and untidy hair—the com- bined effects of weeping and throwing herself down impulsively on the bed. " She's bin a bit upset to- day." " Never mind about her being upset," returned Meldon, good-humouredly, "ask her to come in at once. Say I've got good news, for her." The old lady opened her eyes and trotted off at once, but soon returned, leading in Lizzie, looking very red and very shy, but withal very pretty. Before anything could be said, however, the father came in. The introduction made, Mr. Meldon went on to say : " I have just had a long talk with your brother, Mr. John Collins. He is greatly troubled in his mind about his niece, of whom he is very fond, and he has an idea that somehow his cominr, here to you has brought you all misfortune—baeluck. Of course I do not see how that can be; but one thing I do know' he, poor fellow, has suffered greatly through taking charge of some articles that I had a hand in removing from where they ought to have remained, and I owe him some amends. I have therefore offered him two hundred pounds for those same articles, and here is his 'written authority to hand them to me. Now, it is his wish to give half this sum to his nieee on her marriage, provided you consent to her marrying one named James Watson ; and I will thyself add another hundred pounds, to set the young couple up in housekeeping. Do you consent, Mr. Collins 'r" " Certainly, sir, if that's the case," promptly re- plied the one addressed. And then there was joy in the Collins family, and much kissing between mother and daughter, and much shaking of hands all round. ‘-‘ And now," said Meldon presently, "can you give me that Gold Idol? Your brother said you had. it in sour charge." " Yes, sir, come this way ; it is in an old safe I've got in the other room." , They all went into the next room, and Collins. taking a key from his pocket, opened the " safe," which was a strong, but old and rusty, iron box. But, when he opened it, it was empty! Idol and everything else had vanished !" "Robbed!" yelled Collins, starting back. "Great Heavens ! And now, of course " He glanced despairingly at Melclon. But the latter, instead of looking disappointed, seemed, on the contrary, re-

_ lieved. " Oh, let the pestilent image go !" he cried. " I didn't want it. I was only going to throw it away. I wish joy of it to the thief ; if it brings him the same bad luck it has brought everyone else that has had to do with it, Ido not envy Lim. It shall make no difference to what I promised. I shall pay the money all the same." Then three faces that were beginning to look very glum burst into smiles again. " It's strange that this good luck," said Lizzie, thoughtfully, should come to us just when that gold figure had disappeared. But who can have taken it ?" Then a sudden thought came to her. "Mother !" she exclaimed excitedly, " didn't you, say Tom Benton hadn't been home all night? I see it ! He's the thief !" And she glaneed at her father, who, on his side, looked a bit foolish, and turned his eves from her reproachful 4,taz.a.

No one would have thought a year ago that it would be necessary to appsal to Parliament for a grant to- wards the Queen Victoria Memorial. The King fully expectsd that sufficient funds would be raised by public subscription and his Majesty had hoped to avoid the necessity for seeking the aid of Parliament. So far, [ however, considerably less than £200,000 bas been raised, and a very much larger sum is needed before the Mrmorial Committee can carry out the scheme adopted. As there does not seem any likelihood of this being voluntarily subscribed, it will be necessary to ask tbe House of Commons for a grant, as was the case for

the FriIMO Consort Memorial. Both socially and politically the Lendon season which may be said to commence with tee opening of Parlia- ment, promises to be a very brilliant one. Not enly will there be a great deal of entertaining but the season will be remarkable for the many young and beautiful debutantss, who are waiting to make their appearance in Society. There were no Drawing Rooms last year, and many, who are a little below the usual age, will have exceptions made in their favour, as they are naturally anxious to "come out " during the Corona- tion year. A great many fashionable weddings will also take place during the season and another feature will be the revival of political receptions, at which the Duchess of Devonshire, Lady Tweedmouth, the Duchess of Buccleucb, end Lady Aberdeen, will ba the principal hostesses. In this work Lsdy Aberdeen, seems likely to have the active assistance of her daughter Lsdy Marjorie Gordon, ho is one of the most political minded of the e6butanteF. Towards the end of the month will be cehbrated the Royal wedding in Austria, that of the Archduchess Elizabeth, and it would be quite impossible to enumer- ate the many fashionable weddings that are just now taking place in Landes. Amongst others that will attract a good deal of interest, will be that of Lady Annabel Crewe Milnes, the eldest daughter of Lord Crewe. She is to marry the Hon. erthur O'Neill, and the bride is, of course, a step-daughter of Lady Crewe, the younger daughter of Lord Rosebery. Lady Crewe has unfortunately been far from well since her attack of typhoid fever, and both she and her husband have been a great deal in the doctot's hands since their marriage. One of tbe latest demands of the champions of Women's Rights, in Franca, is that married women ebould retain their maiden names. The wild confusion that would result from:such an innovation is nothing to these French Feminists, who ask if woman is such a chattel that she should lose her identity in marriage. As a matter of fact those women who have made their own name famous, whether on tbe stage or in arts, or literature, do nct lose their identity, and for others, it does not at all matter. The, children, say these advc- eates for progress and reform, should take the names of hen parents, but in course of time the double- barrelled name would become such a many barrelled one, that no visiting card, or gravestone would contain

it. Dancing, it is said, will soon be seen only on the stage. es Hostesees instead of) giving belle, give only dinner parties, and these more often than not, at one or other of the fashionable hotels or restaurants. One reason for dancing going out of fashion tins season, arises from the many people being vaccinated, but it has been steadily declining for years past. The fault of course, rests with the men, as though girls have taken ta cycling and all sorts of outdoor games and recreations, they are as fond of the waltz as ever, but with the men it has become " out of form" to display anything like energy except in the field. At a dance they hang about the doors, or the smoking room, and the principal attraction is the going down to supper. Then young married women often compete for the re ivileges of the girl in the ballroom, but it is net for other pscpie's married daughters that a hostess gives a clence, and what with one adverse tendency and another, denting ' as a fashion has considerably gone out of favour. It is not recorded whether Adam and Eve played with ' a ball, but em doubt there wrra round pebbles in those days, and it is certain that the first kitten discovered their usefulnees as a plaything. It has been the same with the human race. From time immemorial mankind has indulged in some or other game of ball, which in modern times, has come dawn to us in the ebape of cricket, golf, lawn tennis, crcquet, billiards, marbles, and so on. Just now we seem to be in some danger of becoming a nation of " squint eyed ping-pongists." though the game—as it is called—is too silly and childish, to last very long Nevertheless, it has taken a great hold on society, though to see men and women in evening attire indulging In its Infantile excitements, certainly dces provoke some Serious minded people to impatience. Such is the rage for loading the fingers with jewels that gloves are being dispensed with even out of doors, the muff, to some extent, serving as a substitute for the discarded glove. Jewellesy in fact, of all kinds, is being so much worn, that not even the most fortunate and wealthiest possessors, find their stock more than euffioient for their needs. Pearls, for which there has been a great rush have risen to fabulous values, and Sc also have rubies, which are in special request In vi.w of the Coronation. Even the beautiful bet unlucky opals, are being brought forth, as well as turquoises, and other less costly gems. Those who possess great treasures of this kind, need not complain of any want of opportunity for displaying them during the present year. We have had no lack of muddy day 3 this winter, and someone with a liking for figures has calculated that the wemen of London take home on such occasions sorer thing like 30 to 50 tons of dirt on tte3ir skirts and underskirts,. Nevertheless many belonging to the " Smart Sat," continua to wear e.egant frocks, in the lightest and most delicate tones of cloth, to which a Splash of mud means ruination. That of course is all very well for those who can afford tho expense, but those lets favoured with this world's good things should certainly wait until the better weather comes, ere they bedew the fashion in these extravagant tastes. Very tempting are the Brussels shawls,Lirnerick veils, Venetian flounces, and a host of o`her lace articles, set out in fascinating profu3ion in those establishments dealing in such wares, and happy indeed are they who can count such treasures among their " stores." The nomenclature of lace it may interest many to learn, is decided by certain peceliarities of pat ern, mesh, or stitches, that belong to certain localities, and it is retained even when these localities have long ceased to produce their distinctive fabrications. For example, Valenciennes has not for many years wrought the laces that bear its name, their manufacture having long since been transferred to Ypres Belgium, while the Chantilly laces are RII made at Bayeux. Beautiful Irish lace fieured considerably in the trousseaux of Lady Helen Stewart, Lady Gladys Hamilton, and Lady Annabel Crewe Milms, and again this season it pro- mises to be the most worn among all classes of Society, MADGE.

Parr's Bank, Limited.—Report of the Directors. The report and balance sheet of Parr's Bank, Limited, for the year ending 31st December last, has jnst been issued. The annual ordinary general meeting will be held on Thursday next at the Cannon-street Hotel, London —The Directors, in submitting to the shareholders the balance sheet of the bank certified by the auditors, report that the I position and prospects of the business continue to be in every way satisfactory. Including £97,517 17s 6d brought forward at 30th June, 1901, the net balance of profits, alter providing for all had and doubtful debts, end rebating the 'current bills at 5 per cent is .£261,577 Ss 10d. From this sum the directors recommend the payment of a half-year's dividend at the rate of 10 per cent. per annum, payable. free of income tax, on let February, £139,032 lOs ; a bonus of 1 per cent.' payable, free of income tax, on Ist February, £14,635; the transfer to Bank Premises Account, £10,000; total, £163,667 10A, leaving balance to be carried to next account, £97,009 ISs 10d The Directors record, with much regret,the decease of their esteemed colleague, Mr Emil Heinemann, who had been a member of the board since June, 1896. A branch of the bank haA been opened at Llandudno, and a sub-branch will shortly be opened: at West Kirby, Cheshire. The Directors who retire at this time by rotation are Air Edward Banbury, Mr Alfred Crewdscn, Sir J J Harwood, Mr Robert Neill, Mr James Tulloch, and Mr A M Turner, all of whom are eligible for re-election. The Auditors, Messrs Turquand, Youngs, Bishop and Clarke, Lon- don, Messrs Stead. Taylor and Stead, Liverpool, and Messrs Alfred Tongue and Co., Manchester,also retire, and offer themselves for re-election.

- MR. SAM WOODS AND THE NEWTON DIVISION.

- A mining correspondent writes, stating that since his adoption as the Labor.r candidate for the Newton Parliamentary Division of Lancashire, under the miner's labour representative scheme, Majam Woods has not allowed grass to grace under tiiilllllt. Already a num- bfir of meetiugs have been actdressed by Mr. Woods, and his candidature appears to be as bcartily welcomed by Conservative working men throughrut the division as by those who are Literals. There are 12,556 vetors' names upon the register, and only once since 18&5 have the votes for the successful candidate exceeded 5,000. There is almost, if not quite, this number of miners in the constituency, which inclndes the mining vill4gps of Bryn, Haydock, Blackbrook, Rainford, Billings, Buttonwood, COilißS Green, and the outskirts of St Helens. The Earlestuwn Trades Council —Earlestown being tbe headquartrrs of the division— will shortly thten to an address from Mr Woods, and no doubt is entertained as to his adoption. Orgabizaion is to be conducted with vigour, the Lancashire Com- mittee for the promotion of the labour scheme having already appointed Mr William Shaw as registration agent, and he is to commence his duties on thellst proximo. Mr Shaw is an experienced agent, having acted in a aimi'ar capacity in the Ince Division when Mr Woods represented it in the House of Commons. Those who ought to know speak sanguinely of Mr Woods's prospects of success in the Newton Division, _ where be has Hsu d the greater rart of his life.

div.head: CHAPTER V.
div.p: CHAPTER V.

When Meldon and his companion reached the lat- ter's house, a fresh surprise awaited them—a sea- faring man' who had been waiting for an hour or more to seethe Doctor. " I be come about that there Gold Idol as you advertised about," he explained, in a bluff, straight- forward manner. "It don't belong to me, but I can tell ye who it do belong to, and that's two genlemen named Feudal and Meldon; that's the names of the parties I was told to deliver it to." "Then why didn't you do it ?" asked the physician mildly. He could see that the man appeared hon- est enough, though somewhat rough. " This is Mr. Meldou.' "Oh—beg pardin', sir. I didn't know ye. Why didn't I deliver it ? 'Cos I was copped by the In- dians ; carried off, sir. An' there I've been kep' a pris'ner all this time. Only got to the old country t'other day. They thought I 'ad the idol hidden somewhere; but I hadn't. Oh no! I was too fly for that! I'd passed it on to a mate when the Doc- tor, Dr. Elderfield, died—a mate I could trust. An' 'e got clear away with it. An' I got away—in the other direction," he added, ruefully. " Ah, but," he went on cheerfully, " 'twas all for the best, gen'lemen, all for the best. But for that, I should a bin dead, or near dyin', by now; just as
faril
everybody else is 'as touched ha cursed Image. Ay, ay, gen'lemen, I kin tell yer a thing or two about that there _idol as'll,make ye open yer eyes.
An' what's more," he added in a low tone stepping up to Meldon, ''/ kin cure ye—l NOWS the secret !'' "What do you mean, man F" Meldon burst out. " For Heaven's sake don't fool with me! Do you _
say you can cure me—others too! You know—you are sure—?" _ _
.„ . The stranger winked, and nodded his head so continuousbithat he looked like a toy Chinese man- darin. _ _
"All right, gents, make yerselves easy. I under- take to do more 'n the Doctor here can do. I'll cure

ye all—as many as yer likes. Them as poisons kin cure—and—they've told me the secret. In fact they cured me first, so I ought to know !" ,Presently he told his story, which disclosed at its end the secret of the idol's malevolent and apparently supernatural power for evil. Certainly it was an extraordinary tale. Put into plain English, for clearness' sake, it was to the following effect : "My name's Ben Thomas. I went up from Car- acass by the orders of the captain of the ship, with a party of Indians, and a mate, Sam Stevens, to meet the poor old Doctor. But he died just when we got to him. He gave the image and the other articles into my charge, with a paper telling me what to do with them. Take care of them, Ben,' he says, the Indians are after them, and they're not far away.' So I put the things into a rough sack, filled it up with straw, so that it looked like a straw bed, and gave it to an Indian I could trust, and started him and Sam off together. Then, when the enemy swooped down on us' I took up the Doctor's iron box and ran off into the bush with it. That drew the whole yelling pack after me, and let all the rest es. cape. They only wanted the image, and thought I'd got it, for they had traitors in our camp and knew where the Doctor usually kept it. And I knew all about that too—the traitors—and so outwitted them. Well, they marched me off with the box, thinking themselves so jolly safe about it. They didn't even trouble to break the box open for two days—while I was laughing in my sleeve all the time. Then we came to where they had left their chief, named Tracoma, and they presented me to him, box and all. He solemnly ordered the box to oe nroken open very earbflity, and then they found they had been done; and they knew the others had got clear away, and that it was now useless to try to catch them up, for by that time they had got to the boats we had left and were well away down the _ _ _ _ river.
Then theie . was a shindy, I can tell you!

I came in for more kicks than ha'Pence. But, after the first storm was over, and they had decided not to , eat me or roast me alive just than, they settled to carry me back with .them—to have a grander affair , at home, I suppose. But, by the time we arrived there, I had managed to make myself so useful to the chief Tracoma, that he got quite friendly. Then, one day, I saved his life. He was set upon by two tiger cats, and I chipped in and beat them both off. I had no gun—they'd taken that away, of course—only a hunting knife they'd let me have. The beasts had got him drown, and there was no one else near, so I had to do tile best I could. I got badly scratched and bitten myself, but Tracoma was very grateful, and, dfter that, there was no more talk of eating or burning me alive. But they kept me a sort of prisoner; wanted to make me a kind of chief, too. But, in the end, I gave them the slip and got clear away., I had a terrible time though, alone in the wilderness, till I fell in with some friendly Indians 'journeying down to the coast, and they brought me with them to Georgetown. There I got a ship. I managed to bring some gold dust away vaikh me—they've plenty there, those people—and— here I am, gentlemen." 4' But what about the other matter ?" Meldon asked ThoxiMly. • " I'm coming to that, sir ; only I thought I'd ex- plain all the rest first." " It was on the way to the Indian settlement of Leanamouta—we had nearly arrived there—and after the adventure with the tiger cats, that I first began to find out that there was something serious the mat- ter with me : and one day I got so bad, I fell dAwn in a sort of swoon. When I came to mysellB coma was squatting clown beside me, and IA smiled in a queer sort of way. I had bean alje.nein the In- dian country years before, and let Tilt to jabber their language a bit, and I told him I thought I had tht fever. But he shook his head, and gave an nes laugh, and said he knew what it was that ailed me I had been playing, he said, with the golden image, the sacred god,' and the vengeance of the god had fallen on me. But,' he said, ' I can cure you. You saved my life, and. I will do as much for you. My white brother shall find Tracoma is not ungrate- ful. But we must wait until we get home, then shall tell my Kaleema to cure you, and he will do it.' The Kaleema 'is a sort of State poisoner that every chief keeps at hand." " I know," Meldon said. "Go on." " Tracoma's ' Kaleema ' was an old Indian named Samana, and when we arrived at the settlement he took me in hand. I managed to make good friend€ with him, and induced him not only to give me the secret of the antidote, but to tell me all about the old image, and how it poisoned people without their knowing it. The poison is in the hair." Meldon and the Doctor both uttered exclamations of surprise. "How on earth can that be ?" asked Dr. L—. "In this way, sir. Old Samaria, explained it pretty clearly to me. The hair seems to be fine spun gold. but it isn't." " What is it then ?" the physician queried. "That no one knows, sir. But you know what spun glass is like? It can be spun so fine as to seem like soft fine silk or hair, but it is glass all the same ; and is brittle and will break easily, as thin glass always does. Well, the hair of the image seems to be something like that; but what it is made of, or how it was made, no one knows. It was found in the tomb among the ruins in the forest, by the Indians, about a hundred years ago. So far as I understand Samana's description, each bait has many cutting edges. It is shaped, if you could s it under a microscope, I suppose, like a lot of sharp knives placed back to back, with the blades stick- ing out all round in a circle. The spaces betweets the blades are filled with the poison, and when you play with the hair, or turn it about, the little sharp edges cut into tho ,skin, or 'very minute particles breo oft and get into the cracks of the skin, and in title work their way into it, and so poison the bleed. That's how I understand it, sir." Meldon looked at Dr. 44 'What do you think of it ?" he said. "I hardly know: I wish we had the thing here to examine. I wonder what's become of it P" "In the melting-pot by this time—hair and all I expect. We shall toter see it again; but tht thieves will be cruelly punished all the same. don't envy their case. The main thing now is, can this man story about his having the antidote and knowing how to employ it be relied upon 101 l On this point they questioned Thomas closely, bait he adhered confidently to his statements, end was presently sent away with promises of liberal rewards if he cauld make them good. When he had gone, Meldon turned, burning with intense excitement, to the physician. "You don't know what this means to me!'he exclaimed. "1 am engaged to be married SD a young lady lain passionately fella. of, who iS Bhofo returning to England with her father from the Cape. felt that my state I ought not to marry; per- haps even she would not have me, if she were td see me now; or her father would withdra* his consent. Besides, how cola I marry her ?—I--a dying man I had made up my mind to break it off—somehow-- and go abroad and never again return 'to England. In feet I *as making my preparations *hen I saw your advertisement." "Ah !" said Dr. thoughtfully. " now much turns at times upon a trifling matter! This p,ore baneful atata of things....int•—aa alkhas.been

brought ,bbut laiwagn'arhefiladterthrellretEr- Ben Thomas's promises turned out to be no vain boasting, and at the end of a few months Dr. L— bad the satisfaction of pronouncing the opinion that all the victims to the idol's subtle power for evil were restored to health. Meldon called upon him one day to express his gratitude. " I really feel so strongly in this matter," he said, impetuously, "I wish to do something to show my grateful appreciation. The Collins folk are all right and comfortable now—l've seen to that; Watson and Lizzie Collins are married, and I am going to be married. Now what can Ido ?"

" Give me a liberal donation to my hospital," was the Doctor's prompt reply. " Why, yes, of course ! It has all come about through that, and through the kindly interest you take in your poor patients there. It has been a revelation to me ! Somehow, I never before thought much about these institutions. It never occurred to me that I should ever have any personal interest in them." "Yet you have plenty of money, and could very well have afforded to subscribe to our hospital Fund.."

"Well—you see—l never thought about it my- self—and no one happened to ask me." " No," said Dr. with a sigh, " that's just where it is. It is that feeling that makes so many people indifferent, who could give us support if they would, and who really ought to, if you look at it in the proper light. They think hospitals are only of service to the very poor ; there never was a greater mistake ! Any of us, high or low, may find ourselves in a hospital to-morrow. You leave me now in good health and spirits, but, ten minutes hence, you may be run over in the street and be carried unconscious to the nearest hospital." " That's quite true." "Or you may be smashed up in a train—" " Quite true." " Or blown up by an anarchist's bomb, or a gas cylinder, or sizzled on a I?roken electric cable or—" "Thank yOu! You can stop there, I think! There can't be anything worse than that to imagine in your cheerful way." " in not so sure," returned the man of science, with a dry. smile. "You might even—" " lirell—what 2" "Go out to British Guiana again and dig up an- other Gold Idol!"

div.head: IMPORTANT TO WEAVERS. ---- Black burn Girl's Experience.
div.p: IMPORTANT TO WEAVERS. ---- Black burn Girl's Experience.

The need for a steady hand and a col brain on the nart of the weavers in the great cotton factories of Lancashire has been amply demonstrated on many occasions. The working conditions of the cotton opera- tive are of such a nature that the weavers must be possessed of the steady nerves or they are exposed to the danger of accidents at every turn that lurk in the swiftly moviog machinery. A " Blackburn Standard and Express" reporter came across a case the other day where & young weaver had been compelled to pursue her calling for nearly twelve months with her system so racked with pain that en many occasions she load fallen on to the looms under her charge, and had several times had narrow escapes from being seriously injured. The young lady's name is Miss Jane Clarke. She is twenty- two years of age, and she lives with her mother and sisters at 187 Accrington-road, Blackburn. " For nearly twelve months," said Miss Clarke in answer to the interviewer, " I was ill, having a racking pain in my side, which used to stop my breathinv. I had medical advice from time to time, and sometimes got relief, but the cure was never permanent and the old pain returned. My mother tried plasters of all sorts on my back and side, and I tock different kinds of pine but none of them did me any good. I gradually got into a very low state, and used to turn giddy ; in fact I fell over my borne many a time, and I was fortunate to escape accident." "And did this state of affairs continue all the time ?"

inquired the reporter. " Yes ; for the whola of the time I have mentioned and then it wail that lea w Dr Williams' pink pills for pale people highly spoken of in the newspapers." "And am I right in assuming that your present satisfactory state of health is duo to Dr Williams' pink pills ?" "Yes," interposed Mrs Clarke, who was present during the interview," ehe took the pills, and after the first box I asked her if she felt any improvement and the replied that she thought she did. She continued to take the pills, with what result you can see." " How many boxes have you taken altogether, Miss Clarke ?'' I "About ten, I think ; but you know lam persevering with then'. After the first two or three boxes I f elt great deal better, and I am wonderfully improved, the pain having left me, and I can go about my work with out pain or fear." ":And you are perfectly willing that your experience should be published ?" "I am," was the ro ady reply. "Dr. Williams' pink Dills for pale people have done me a great deal of good. and I would have other p(ople know how they might be cured from pain similar to that which I suffered." Do you know of anyone else who has derived bene- fit by taking Dr. Williams' pink pills ? " The question was answered by Mrs Clarke as follows : "Oh, yes. My daught'T Ann, who is eighteen years of age, began to take the pills cu firding that they did her sister good. She had a ..kio trouble,and I must say the pills have also done her good." Before leaving the house the reporter ascertained that Mies Clarke followe 1 her occupation as a weaver lat Messrs Birtwistl., Marsden and Riley's Alexandra, I Mil'.

TRADING. The Action for Slander against Mr. John Pemberton.
We understand that the action for slander brought by Councillor F R Roberts against Mr John Pemberton, of Stockton Heath, will be heard at Manchester Assizes at the end of this month.
:Alderman J. Shaw Green and Mr. Dodds.

TO THE EDITOR OF THE WARRINGTON "EXAMINER." Sir,—Will you allow me to correct one of the statements of Alderman J:Shaw,Green in the Council Chamber on Tuesday last as reported in the War- rington " Guardian " of Januars Sth. He stated that Mr Dodds had resigned his appointments in the Wesleyan Church, and that this was done to prevent an official enquiry by a Court of the Church of which Alderman J Shaw Green, Councillor Brongh end Mr Dodds were members. Mr Dodds has not held any appointments in the Wesleyan Church for more than two years What he did was to.resign his membership of the Church. My relations with Mr Dodds have been of a con- fidential nature for many years. We have often discussed the reasons for the step he has now taken. For more than two years he has been strongly of the opinion that holding the views he does on certain matters of Church policy be ought not to allow hisdiame to remain on a Methodist class book. It is only against his better judgment and on the advice of several friends that he has deferred taking the step until now. Without endorsing Mr Dodds' action or other- wise may Ibe allowed to say that holding the views he does, he could no', in justice to himself do other than he has done.—Yours truly, JOHN UPSON. Orford Villas.
Rejoinder by Mr Dodds.
TO THE EDITOR WARRINGTON " EXAMINER."

Sir,—Tuesday's meeting of the Town Council will I think prove histtrical; it marks the parting of the ways—the tardy yet healthy mutiny of the more independent members against the tyranny of the now notorious and discredited compact which for over four years has fostered so appalling an amount of crooked, immoral and illegal treding on the part of many aldermen and councillors with the Cor- poration. We shall await with interest the fate of Mr Councillor Pierpoint's motion in its present or amended form at the next Council meeting, and we may safely leave the pulverisation of the rill' c- ulous resolution of the General Purposes Committee to the next public meeting to be held under the auspices of the Municipal Non-Trading Committee. The speeches generally may also be left over to the same occasion, or consigned to a merciful ob- livion, but as a gratuitous personal attack was made upon me, I feel that any delay in replyingl thereto might be misunderstood. No doubt, if all 1 your readers were well acquainted with Alderman' Shaw:Green it would be quite unnecessary tor me to notice his characteristically disingenuous remarks, as to such readers they carry with them their own antidote. There are, no doubt,a few, however, who do not understand that gentleman's methods, and for their enlightenmerrt, let me say a few words. And first with regard to Buckley and Co, Ltd.—l have to say that I have done nothing more than name in one letter and in one speech,thae Company along with two or three others whose shares were largely held by members ofithe Council, and which were dealing largely with the Corporation. It is true that on very propergrounds the head of one of the Pearson and Knowles' departments some 12 or 13 years ago, stopped the carts of Buckley and Co. from entering their works. It is also true that on April 10th, 1889, shortly after he entered the Council, Mr Shaw Green wrote me a personal letter telling me that three or four:friends including him- self had turned George Duckley'e business into a limited liability company, that he Mr Green was the secretary, that Mr Thomas Hall of Monks Hall and Co.. was the chairman, and that their carts had been refused. entrance to our works. To show that Mr Shaw Green then knew that I had nothing to do with the matter, I quote the concluding sent- ence of his letter. It reads " personally I should take it as a favour if you would kindly put these circumstances before the gentleman who has charge of the department." On receipt of this letter I at once enquired into the matter, and finding that the 'refusal was most proper, and such as no business Iman could do other than approve, 1 wrote to Mr Green on April 12th, 1889 that "I was sorry the matter could not be re-opened."—Since that date, now nearly 13 years ago. I have never heard another word upon the subject. It was in no way in my control, and indeed, until I read the speech of Mr Green in last Wednesday's "Guardian" and had looked up the correspondence I have referred to, I had forgotton the entire circumstances Now for the reference to the Wesleyan Society, and the alleged attack upon Mr Brough and Mr Green which the latter says resulted in Mr Brough and himself feeling that they were both injured in their characters—and both thought that their proper course as honest men was to ask for an enquiry and the fullest investigation l "They were preparing themselves" (continued Mr Green) "for such an inquiry, and what did they think happen- ed ! Mr Dodds sent in his resignation of the appointments he held, and thereby prevented them bringing him before the court of enquire." I put it to you and your readers, that the only reasonable interence to be drawn from Mr Green's words just quoted is that on hearing that Mr Brough and Mr Green had taken steps to bring me before some Wesleyan Church Court, I, in the most cowardly way sent in my "resignation of the ap- pointments I held" in the Wesleyan Society in order to avoid such on ordeal ! ' Now, Sir, for the facts. let. It is over 2 years since I resigned every " appointment I held in the Wesleyan Society," and on December 4th last I retired from the private membership of our Pen- keth resident minister's Society Class, the meetings of which I have never once attended. 2nd. Until I read Mr Green's speech, I had never heard a sug- gestion of any desire for such an enquiry on the , part of Messrs Brough and Green. 3rd. I have since interviewed the official Warrington Wesleyan , Circuit Secretary, and find no notice had been given to him a any enquiry, nor did he know of 'any Court for the purpose named. nor had he heard lof any such thing being contemplated. I have also enquired of several leaders of the Wesleyan Church, and in nct a sirele instance had a whisper been heard of any such proposal until Mr Green's speech appeared in the newspapers. Bat to show the hollowness of this proposed desire for any enquiry and that thine has never been the shadow of a pretext for constituting it, let me state that I have never once during the agitation mentioned Mr Brough's name in any shape or form. So much in regard to Mr Brough. with whom I had a triendly chat on Tuesday morning last, and whose views are largely in harmony with my own, as shown by his letter to the public meeting of October 30th last, in which he wrote "I don't believe in any member of the Town Council using his pesition for private ends, they are the servants of the public, and all they do should be done in the interests of the public they represent." Neither in regard to Mr Green is there anything I have said which could possibly be made a pretext for any such en- quiry as has been eukgested. I wrote in June last, that the " Tinnion enquiry" into the charge against Mr Green should have been carried further, as it was absolutely clear from the committee's report that the Cor- poration irregularly paid him £lO 10, and I have also said that as the Secretary and the third largest shareholder in John Buckley and Co„ Limited, 'which compeny received £2,250, on the last two municipal years, for carting, etc. I considered Mr len to be in a wrong position. Does Mr Green fly that the committee reported he had -.Kularly received the £lO 103 ;does he deny that 011dsetr% secretary and the third largest share- ' Buckley and Co?—lf not, end if I have never even way b mentioned Mr Brown name in any ow ean it be seriously said that there is anything at all upon which a church court could adjudicate? Ir Green must know that there is not; and he also knows perfectly well that I could not possibly have had any idea tbat be and Mr Brough contemplated seeking a church enquiry at the time I decided to retire from the private mem- bership of the Wesleyan Society. The reasons I gave for my retirement were that for some years past I bad" been out of sympathy with the action and attitude of Wesleyaniem in re- gard to many matters, and that I felt I was in a wrong position." Sir, it is painful to have to go into these personal matters, but I will make a clean breast of the busi- nese.—At the begiunin g of last year I promised to

I paid this sum on the 4th December, and on the same day I wrote the Rev John Gunnell, with a further sum due from rne under another head on the 16th De- cember, and took the opportunity of retiring from membership, a step which for obvious reasons I did not care to take earlier. lam still a seatholder, and it has been my intention to continue to support as hitherto, but from a position of greater freedom and less responsibility such of the Wesleyan insti- tutions as commend themselves to me. It is said that "suspicion haunts the guilty mind." I begin to think the members of the Council cannot realise that anyone can take part in the " No Trading" agitation from pure motives. The ex-Mayor vainly tried to drag a herring across the path; now Mr Shaw Green has still more miserably and deservedly failed in a similar effort. His objects indeed have been too transparent; he knew that in regard to anything I had said or done in respect of Mr Stough and himself there was not the slightest work for a church enquiry and that he could not secure one ; he knew that it was im- possible I could have had the least idea that he was seeking an enquiry when I retired from the " private membership," is it not clear that his ends have been, to create an impression that I ran away from an enquiry, and to bring before the W es- leyans of Warrington, in a way which might damage my influence, that I was not any longer a member with them?—l am, ,tc., JAMES DODDS. div.head: LATE MR. JOHN CROSFIELD, J.P.
div.p: THE LATE MR. JOHN CROSFIELD, J.P.
Memorial Service at the Workingmen's
M:ssion.

There was a crowded congregation at the Working- men's Mission on Sunday evening, when a memorial service to the late Mr John Crosfield, JP, was held. No doubt many of our readers will remember that the mission was established by Mr Crosfield and others over thirty years ago, and those who have carried on the week of the mission have re eeived much valuable assist- ance from Mr Crosfield from time to time. The news of Mt Crosfield's death was received with deep regret by the members of the congregation and the large attendance at the service on Sunday was evidence of the respect entertained for the deceased gentleman. Among those present were : Mrs Crosfield, Mr George Cromfield, Miss Gertrude Crosfield, Mr Kipps (head , gardener at Walton Lea) and Mrs Kipps. Appropriate hymns were feelingly sung by the congregation and the choir rendered the anthems, 66 Hallelujah" and 66 The radiant morn "In a very creditable manner.

Mr. THO'AAS DALE delivered an address during the course of which he said they had met that evening in sorrow and bereavement. As citizens they felt they bad sustained, in the death of Mr. Crosfield, an irreparable loss, but as worshippers at that mission the loss was felt more acutely. They thought it was their duty to hold that simple service to show their deep gratitude to their late beloved patron. He had selected a passage from which to speak, namely the words "The memory of the just 19 blessed." Tbe wisest man—the wisest they supposed Weo ever lived—spoke those beautiful words, and wuen he gave utterance to them he had, in his mind's eye, one of the noblest characters that had 'preceded him. That character had begun in human life, but God called him to a higher position and he eventually sat upon a throne. Mr Crosfield was a man of peace. He did not occupy a throne but he , occupied the best place in the hearts and affections of his townsmen. Ms life was filled with noble deeds. As a businees man he was successful in the undertaking with which his name was identified, and as a politician , he was a pronounced Liberal. The best politicians were men whose souls were inflaenced by that higher power. Would to God they had more Christian men as rulers of this country. Mr Crosfield was 01:13 who had tried to serve his town in the Coined Chamber, and while there honours were repeatedly conferred upon him. He was exalted te the highest positien in the Town Council, mayor and chief magistrate. Further, he was made a freeman of the Borough. All that went to show that their noble patron had been engaged in the social well-being of the town in which he lived and loved. He (Mr Crosfield) was & lover of pictures, and his impres- sion, after a visit with other members of the church, to Walton Lea, was thatithe study of pictures was one of his chief delight!. He also loved flowers, and took a great delight in the cultivation of the rarest varieties. He realized the pleasures he had himself and immensely increased them by allowing his townmen to go and view the same beauties. Their late patron was also a lover of children. He had given the schools in Thewlis-street, which would remain an everlasting monument to his name. Mr Croafield had been with them in that house of prayer and listened to their simple songs and messages Mr T. ASHLEY also delivered an address. He said their meeting that night was for the purpose of paying a tribute of respect and love for one whose loss they felt as of a father or a brother. Their hearts were full of sympathy for those who mourned. At the fireside there was now a vacant chair; the loving voice which had cheered and helped was now silent, and they earnestly prayed that the Father of all would go to the heart and home of those who sorrowed, and apply, the healing balm that human love and sympathy failed to give. Their esteemed patron, Mrs Crosfield, was a broad-minded man with large beart and generous spirit. He ever sought to help those who were in hard or humble circumstances, and wan essentially a man of peace. Re was always to the front in matters of education, and ever strove for the betterment and liberty of the masses. Mr Crosfield, along with a few other willing workers established that mission over 30 years ago, and eternity alone would reveal the lives which had been brightened through his unswerving effort; in that particular parish which gave him birth. At the laying of the foundation atone in 1871 he said he hoped that mission would be a comfort and a blessing to the neighbourhood, and at the opening of the new schools in 1899 (28 yea's after) he remarked that the mission had been tht ice blessed, firstly to the children, secondly to the teachers, and also to the parents, to know that their children were being trained in the fear of the Lord, which afforded him boundless satisfaction. Mr Crosfield's desire was that the mission should be strictly unseetarian, only aiming at the uplif;eng of the people, and the glory of God. They as a congregation bad great cause of gratitude for all the kindness and help' he had afforded to that mission year after year. They had great cause to thank God they ever knew him. They could not re-3all him, but they could follow bie noble example. In conclusim, he exhorted those present to be "steadfast and immovable.always abound- ing in the work of the lend ; for, as they knew, labour for the Lord was not in vain." At the conclusion of the address, Mr Atkinson, the oerflgeaendmstely.ptihayeeedo ntghree g tei ao dn stanrdcihngi " .n The s Saul" y n' ovuenrc. ing of the Benediction concluded the service.

Yesterday morning a boy walking down St. Martin's- lane, London, discovered a human head lying in tbe gutter. He conveyed it to the Westminster Hospital, where be was advised to take it to a police station, which he accordingly did, carrying tbe head under his arm to Bow.street Police Court. A surgeon was sum- moned, and pronounced the head to be that of an elderly mon. The head was afterwards conveyed to the mor- tuary at florseferry-lane, where it awaits an inquest. The head, whicn is nearly black, has not apparently been used for anatomical purposes.

div.head: DEATH OF MR. JOHN PEERS, OF PEN KETH.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. JOHN PEERS, OF PEN KETH.

To readers of this journal, the name of Mr. John Peers will have become familiar, in consequence of the many letters which have appeared over his name in our correspondence columns on religious and other questions. This week it is our painful duty to record his death, which occurred with startling suddenness on Saturday afternoon last. During the preceding week he appeared to be in his usually good state of health. On the previous Thursday he had cycled to Liver- pool, and on Friday last he walked from his residence, the Hawes, Penketh to Warrington, and transacted business here. He was taken ill at about six o'clock on Saturday morning. The symptoms did not point to anything of an alarming nature and when asked if a doctor should he called in he replied that he did not think one was neces- sary. Towards noon he became worse, and Dr Murray was sent for but before the medical gentle- man arrived, Mr Peers expired in a chair. He was sixty-three years of age, and a widow and four children survive him. Mr Peers was the son of the late Mr John Peers, a maltster,whose place of business was in the build- ing now used by the Salvation Army in Warrington as a barracks. He was born in Buttermarket-street, where he resided for many years. He subse- vently removed to Hale and then to Penketh. He was a gentleman or independent means and owned censiderable property in Warrington and neighbourhood. He was devoted to outside pur- suits and was an enthusiastic yachtsman and cyclist. He was a member of the Warrington Field Club, from its inception and during the last session he read a paper entitled " A Siesta,' in which he recounted his voyaging in the" Woodcock" a boatwhich he owned and in which he spent many happy hours. He was one of the oldest managers of the Warrington Savings Bank and for many , years he had been a member of the Museum Com- mittee of the Warrington Corporation. He did not take an active part in public affairs, but in politics he was a sound Liberal. He was better known as a controversialist in newspaper corres- pondence on religious and other questions. He ad- vocated a wide freedom in religious thought, and his letters on vaccinatien showed him to be a strong anti-vaccinator. THE FUNERAL. The grave closed over the remains of Mr Peers on Wednesday afternoon. The interment took place at Great Bankey Cemetery in the presence of a num- ber of sorrowing friends. The ceremony at the graveside was conducted by the Rev John Gunnell, Wssleyan minister. The coffin was borne to its last resting place by a number of fellow yachtsmen on the river, namely : Messrs W Knowles, J Moss, T Mose, T Whittle, H Turner, and R Daintith. The chief mourners were Mrs Peers (widow), and Mr John Peers (son). The Museum Committee, of which Mr Peers was a member, was represented at the funeral by Mr W Monks (chairman),Alderman F W:Monks, Alderman J Shaw Green' Councillor Greening, Councillor Ellison, and Mr Charles Madaley (librarien). There were also present Mr Charles White (chairman of the Warrington Field Club), Mr lhomas Tunstall (actuary of the Warrington Savings Bank), Mr R Garnett, J.P.. Mr W Furness, Mr Jackson, Mr J Sherlock, Mr J Clare, Mr J S Snoddy, and Mr W Rowe. Wreaths had been sent by "Thomas and J Moss," Mr and Mrs Moss, Mr and Mrs J S Snoddy.

div.head: GOOD TEMPLARS' CONVENTION
div.p: GOOD TEMPLARS' CONVENTION
AND CONFERENCE.

The usual monthly meetiug of the No. 1 Convention of S.W. Lancashire Good Templars was held in Hope Hall, Wigan, on Saturday last, when there was an unusually large attendance of representatives from lodes at Wigan, Hindley, Leigh, Ashton, Earlestown, Widnes, and St. Helens, as well as • number of distin- guished officers and visitors from Liverpool and Charley. The Cocvention was opened by Bro George Clarke, C C, of Earlestown, at 3.40 p.m. The usual Reporting and Credential Committees were appointed, after which the Convention Secretary (13z0 P Smith) gave an interesting monthly report, and was followed by the Convention Visiting Officer, who reported on their quarter's visita- tion of the various lodges, and which showed general activity and much good work done. Arrangements are being made to re-start lodges at Atherton and Tyldesley in a few weeks.—After general discussion reports were adopted, with thanks to officers for their good work.—The distinguished viaitore were then for- mally introduced and heartily welcomed to the Conven- tion, and:were as follows :—Bro Rev J A Lee, DC T, Bre G B Walker, D f, Sister Mrs Walker, DV T, Bro Alfred A Lee, all of Liverpool ; Bro W Retcliffe, 13r0 A Ashton, Sister Miss Birch, of Cttorley.—Bre Lee was invi- ted to preside for the remainder of the Session. Earnest and encouraging addre-ses were then given by the visi- tors, Bro Ratcliffe of Charley'tendering good wishes and greetings from Bra A E Eccles, P.G., treasurer, of IChorley who had very generously sent a large parcel of ' valuable and useful books and pamphlets for free dis- tribution to those attending the conventionalr arty' thanks being accorded to Bro Eccles for his kindness and generosity. A vote of sympathy was expressed and ordered to be sent to Bro Morris Jones, D.S., of Liver- pool, who was unable to be present through illness. The next seseion was arranged for Whines on February Bth, and an invitation to meet at Earlestown on March Bth was accepted. Business over an excellent paper was read by Bro E Newman, D.S.J.T , on" How to improve our sessions." Some interesting and useful hints and suggestions were given which were freely com- mented on in a good discusssion which followed. Thanks of the Convention were accorded the essayist, who responded. Thanks were also tendered to the visitera who had encouraged them by their presence and council, and to the Wigan friends for the arrangement for the Session of the Convention which was closed at 5.40, to partake of a nicely laid tea on the kind invita- tion of the Officers of the South West Lancashire District Lodge At 7 p.m. a r3onference was held to eoasider the " Good of the Order" in the area of the Convention. Bro Rev J A Lee D.C.T., presided, supported by the officers of the District Lodge and No 1 Convention. The Chairman in introducing the subject for discussion said although in a few places they would be glad to bear of a better state of things still generally, in eeeir district good solid work was being done, L Agee were showing signs of improvement,several new Lodges werseabout t be opened and there was very much to encourage them to go fforward. The district executive were arranging for a similar conference in Liverpool during next week, and had several important mission efforts in hand from which they hoped for good results, and in concluding remarks he said in that Conference he wished them to consider.-1, proepeetive places where new lodges might be opened or sleeping ones revived ; 2, how can we best help those lodges that just now appear weak and need invigorating ; and 3, what other aggreesive measures can be suggested for this area, that can be carried out during the next two months. A most earnest and animated discussion followed in which the foregoing and other useful points were brought out amongst those taking part being the following. Bros A Travers, George Clarke, E Newman and Sister Dare Francis of Earlestown, Bro George Brooks and J Hulme of Leigh, J Lindon and Jl3 Turner, of St. Helens. J Vint, and J Speakman, and P Smith of Ashton-in- Maeerfield. Bro. A A Lee and Sister Mrs Walker of Liverpool, Bros. Ratcliffe and Ashton of Chorley, the chairman calling upon Bro. G B Walk rr of Liverpool to close the discussion which had been full of interest ell throrigh. Special committees were appointed to take immediate action in various places, from which it is fully anticipated practical good will follow. On the motion of Bro. George Clarke,seconded byliro AfFrancis hearty thanks were accorded the district officers for their kind entertainment and very valuable and en- couraging visit to the Convention, and a most iospiring and enthusiastic series of meetings were brought to a close with the Doxology and Benediction.

div.head: Sr. PETER'S CIIOIIAL SOCIETY, NEWTON.
div.p: Sr. PETER'S CIIOIIAL SOCIETY, NEWTON.

The first annual soiree in connection with the above Society, was held in the Town Hall, Newton, on Friday evening, The attendance of members and friends was very good, but the hall was not too crowded for comfortable dancing, and it proved to be one of the most ;select Eand enjoyable dances of the season. The room was artistically decorated by a few willing helpers, and a number of plants were kindly lent by Mrs Gillespie. Dancing com- menced at 8 o'clock, to the music of Peplow's band. During the first interval, the Misses Sweetiove gave the duet " Convent Bells," and at the second interval Miss Adams:entertained the company with the song "Green Isle of Erin."

Street Improvements at Golborne.

At the Warrington County Petty Sessions on Wednesday the magistrates (Captain Withington and Mr J Ball) decided an objection which was 1 made to certain proposals of the Golborne Urban District Council under the Private Streets Works Act, by the Albion Brewery Company.—Mr T Ellis appeared on behalf of the Council and the Brewery Company was represented by Mr Darlington—Mr Ellis said the proposals of the Council werein regard to street improvements,and embraced two streets— Heywood-street and Manners-street There were no objectors in regard to the latter street. The Council intended to pave, channel, curb and 'make good the streets. The owners of property in Heywood street were Messrs Richard Evans and Company and the Albion Brewery Company and the former offered no ob- jection to tbe scheme. The Brewery Company I objected, on the grounds that the provisional apportionment of the cost was incorrect.—Mr. Darlington said the company were the owners of a cottage which had been converted into a public house. They contended that Messrs Evans who were the owners of twenty cottages made twenty times as much use of Heywood-street as the Brewery Company. He submitted that a local authority had no right to arbitrarily say that a frontage owner should pay one half the cost irres- pective of what use he made of the street. Toe amount which the company were asked to pay was £5B 14s 31.—M r Ellis said that Messrs Evans and the Brewery Company bad the same length of frontage.gMessrs Evans, however,had only a piece of vacant land fronting 61eywood-street and the chief feature of the street was that it afforded a means of access to the side entrance of the public house and led ronnd to a back passage to the , cottages. It could not be suggested that the cot- tages would be benefited by the improvement as the one object the tenants would have in going round the back passage would be to get to the public house. After hearing evidence the magistrates made an order for the payment of the full amount— £5B 14s 3d by the company.

Warrington Boy's Sad Death. The sad death of :boy named Thomas Henry Walton (13), who rosld3d at 2, Stamford-street,War- ington, formed the subject of an inquest conducted at the Police Station on Monday afternoon by Mr S Brighouse, county coroner.—From the evidence it appeared that the deceased in company with Walter Summerfield and Joseph Clare went to Longford Gas Works in a cart belonging to Messrs Naylor and Walton on Saturday morning to obtain load of mortar. On arriving at the works de- ceased Was left in the cart alone and it seems that he got out nf the vehicle and mounted the horses back. The animal commenced to run and deceased was thrown to the ground, the wheel of the cart passing over his neck. He was picked up by a man ' named Robinson, who is employed at the works, and Dr Curtis was sent for, but on his arrival life wasfound to be extinct. A verdict of " Accidents death " was returned.

_ . The annual general meeting of the Sankey Wire Mills Cricke:, Club was held on Monday last in the Coffee Tavern' Liverpool-road, there being good attendance. Mr Frank Williams occupied the chair. A letter was read from the President, Mr Samuel tiough‘on, regretting he was unable to attend, but wished the club a prosperous season. The Chairman then delivered a short address, after which the usual business was gone through. The Secretary reported that the Ist Eleven had pla3ed 18 matches last year, wan 11. last 4 and drawn 3. The 2nd Eleven bad played 12, won 10, lost 2. The balance sheet was read by the treasurer, Mr James Evans, and it showed that the club was in a very flourishing condition. A vote of thanks was given to the presi lent, patrons, vice-presidents of the club I for their assistance last year. The following is a list, of officers appointed for the coming season. Presi- dent, Mr E Houghton; all the vice-presidents were again re-elected. Captain Ist eleven Mr W Wood- cock ; Sub-captain let eleven, Mr H Clarke; captain 2nd eleven, Mr F Clegg; sub-captain 2nd eleven, Mr J Barlow; treasurer, Mr James Evans ; com- mittee, Messrs W Backhouse, H Clarke, G Gough,'J Hawthorn, T Barlow, J Monks and J J Pritchard; secretary, Robert W Cook ; umpire Ist eleven, Mr J Sutton ; scorer Ist eleven, Mr IV Backhouse Umpire 2nd eleven, Mr W Wilkes ; scorer 2nd eleven, Master A Cook. A vote of thanks to the chairman ended the meeting._ _

Warrington Board of Guardians. A meeting of this Board was held in the Board Room at the Workhouse, on Wednesday. Mr A J Jolley presided and there were also present: Mrs Clay, Bev Father Wilson, Dr Murray, Messrs T H Ashcroft, J Payton, Robinson, William Houghton G:Pilling,J Clarke, William Mather,A Brookes,with J C 'Sutton (clerk), and A Wright (superintendent Padgate schools).—The Padgate Schools Committee recommended that the tender of Messrs Williams and Clay for a new range and boiler in kitchen No. 4, including cost of fixing at £l6 ss. be accepted. This was agreed to.—Mr William Houghton asked whether the Board bad any voice in recommending suitable cases for Winwick Asylum.—The Chair— man said it was the intention of the Asylums Board to admit only chronic cases at the new asylum and these would be taken from the other asylums in the county—Mr William Houghton said they bad several chronic cases in the Asylums and be thought they might make a recommendation con- cerning them. The Clerk advised that when the deputation from the Board visited the asylums they might speak with the superintendent's res- pecting such cases.— Mr William Houghton said there was another matter he wished to refer to. They bad signed the contracts that morning for two vaccination officers. He understood that the latt Vaccinatian Act was only passed au' the understanding that it was in the nature of an experiment for five years, and he would like to know how much of that period had run —Mr Pilling said the Act was passed ia 1898.— Mr Houghton thought the Board ought to take some steps towards getting a revision of the scale of fees. They had passed a monstrous bill that morning for vaccination fees. He would suggest that they start a movement throughout the country for a revision of the fees. Mr Pilling said many Boards of Guardians throughout the country had appealed to the Government on the question, The Clerk thought thelproper place to discuss the subject was at the meetings of the Poor Law Association - There they hart a representative gathering of the poor law guardians, and any decision come to on the matter might have an influence on Parliament. Resolutions by individual Boards of Guardians had not the same influence.—Mr Houghton: I hope the Boards of Guardians will have had enough of the vaccination Act in five years. Mr Pilling said he was present at the meet- ing of the Runcorn Board of Guardians on the pre- vious day and the Board decided to support a • resolution of the Cardigan Board asking the Government to revert to the old system. The clerk: It is really a Parliamentary matter.—The matter , then dropped.

div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
;-'Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.

There was an average attendance at the meeting of this society on Saturday afternoon. Mr Pickavance presided and delivered a brief address on " The Crea- tion." The speaker for the occasion was Mr Barbery, of Oldharn, who based a thoughtful addrees on the teat "Consider the Li 11!..." Mr Walter Clay sang as a solo "Sun Of my Su!." The service was also taken pert ia by Mr Thomas Hawthorn and Mr B Farrar ;hon. Ee ;re- taryl.
The Evangelical Free Church Council.

A very satisfactory week of universal prayer, under the auspices of the Warrington Evangelical Free Church Council, concluded on Saturday evening. There have been good attendances at the meetings and a great deal of benefit has been derived. On Sunday, the annual ' exchange of pulpits took place. The allocations of the Free Church ministers of the town were as follow Bswsey-road Wesleya.n, Rev J S Elaghes ; 13)1d-street ' Wesleyan, Rev E T Reed ; Emmanuel Reformed Epis- copal. Rev J F Matthews ; hill Cliffe Baptist. Rev C Finch • St. John's Presbyterian, Rev C H Hocken ; Latchenrd Baptist, Rev .1 L Mime; Legh-street Primi- tive Methodist, Rev W C J Nsville ; Sankey Bridges Wesleyan, Rev J Yonge ; Wycliffe Cengregational, Rev T Bishop. The annual united communion service was held at a later hour the same evening in the Bewsey-road Wesleyan Cnurch. There was a large congregation,:all the Free Evangelical Churches of the town being represented. The service, which was a very impressive one was conducted by the 113 V C H Hocken, and the elements were handed round by the ministers of the Free Churches. The Rev J L Milne delivered an address, in which he referred to the need for greater unity amongst Christian Churches. Prayers were offered by the Rev J F Matthews and the Rev John Yonge. The singing was led by the BeweeN- road Wesleyan choir, under the conduct orship of Mr Wadsworth:

New Organ at St. Clement's Mission. On Sunday last the new organ which has recently been erected in Sc Clement's Mission, Warrington, was dedicated for use in the ssrvices of the miFsion. The instrument which is described as "The Positive Organ" (Casson's patent) is designed by the well-known expert, Mr Thomas Casson, for Country, Mission and Colonial Churches or other places where a skilled organist is not al map available, or where an instrument of greater importance weuld be too large or costly. The tones are produced by real organ pipes exclusively. It has so free " reeds " such as are used for the harmonium or the form of harmonium known as an " American Organ." By special mechanism anyone who can play correctly on the pianoforte an ordinary hymn tune can ,do so on the " Positive " with the effect of a skilled pelf =arm° on an organ of two manuals and pedals. and can also traespose. The following is the specifica- tion :—Open diapason (through) BFt pitch. spotted metal ; salicional, tenor f. grooved to No 3, B,t pitch, spotted metal ; gedeckt bass, gedeckt treble, eft pitch, wood; dulcet bass, dulcet treble, 4f5 pitch, spotted metal ; bourdon treble, 1610 pitch, spotted metal ; bass, 16ft pitch, spotted metal ; melodic diapason, Bft pitch, spotted metal ; transposer, composition knee lever.—The organ was used for the first time at the choral celebration of the Holy Communion at 8 a.m. when there was a good congregation. Mr F M Derby, organist at the Parish Churcb,ably presided at the instrument. The other services of the day were %eel attended,the mission being completely filled in the evening. The service was eonducted by the Rev A S Cameron, and the prayers were read 1)5 the Rev Morley Steveneon. The Ray A A Markham, of St Jude's, Liverpool (formerly in charge of the mission),presided at the organ with great ability, and also preached the sermon taking for his text the , words "Rejoice at the sound of the organ"—Job xxi.32. An able description of the development of the organ from the primitive reeds was given, and the preacher showed what purooms the instrument served in Divine worahip.—The Rev A S Cameron explained that the actual cost of the organ had been defrayed, but a con- siderab!e sum was still required to pay for its erection, the alterations to the wall and the removal of certain seats.—The choir gave a very creditable interpretation of the anthem "I will magnify Thee."

Boots Circulating Library. A circulating library has °been established by Boots Limited at their shop, 5, Bridge-street. A monthly list of the newest books is published and subscribers may obtain books on the following terms :—For one volume at a time, 2s GI a month, Gs for six months, or 10s Gi for a year. For three volumes at a time, one month ss, six months 129, and twelve months £1 Is. For the convenience of those 'rho do not wish to take out a subscription the new, as well as the old books, may be borrowed by the day and by the week.
