div.p: citizen as worker is therefore already a serious matter; and, indeed, the organisations of retail confections and allied trades are already demand- ing the removal of a burden which has gravely injured them. But cheap sugar, besides giving us one of our most valuable food- stuffs, and finding employment in various directions for very large numbers of hands, has become the raw material of great export trades which would be destroyed by any such handicap as is now proposed. We have heard a great deal lately of the Government's tenderness towards the West Indian planters and the British refiners--two small groups of men whose interests sink into insignificance besides those of the traders in raw sugar and the makers of confectionery, biscuits, jam, the fruit-growers, box-makers, and a , score of connected businesses at home. Why should these men be singled out to bear the bur- dens which an inept Cabinet has accumulated? The question holds good for the other commod:ties we have mentioned as already marked for attack. If there were no untouched sources of revenue: in a country that is still and after all the wealthiest in the world we could understand Sir ROBERr GIFFEN'S attitude. The case being of so very ' different a complexion, it is difficult to suppose that his revolutionary appeal can have any success. All the same, it would be well that those who still cherish ideas of honesty and impartiality in finance, even when circumstances make actual retrenchment Ptnpossible, should realise the danger that lies immediately ahead, and concert measures to effectively combat it.

LORD ROSEBERY, unlike Lord Rosebery's Mr BALFOUR, reads the Position. newspapers. He is there- fore acquainted both with the text of Sir HENRY CAMPBELL-BANNERMAN'S speech and the opinions of the Liberal Press on the question of his return to active work for the party. He has no reason to complain of the tone of the appeal, nor can he find in it any qualification to embarrass him or cause him to hesitate. The most Radical of London morning papers, which has taken a strong line on the war, has gone out of its way to empha- sise its appreciation of his "brilliant intellect " and the value of his "ripe experience." There can be no doubt that his co-operation, besides adding largely to the fighting power of the Opposition, would have a steadying effect on the section with which he has least in common. Mr LLOYD-GEORGE, Sir ROBERT REID, and Mr BRYCE, for example, welcomed the Chesterfield speech with an ardour which was sincere and unmistakable, and every day has made more apparent that the differences of the Liberal party in reality appertain to events that are past and irrevocable, and that, in regard to the South African question as it stands to-day, there is substantial agreement. It was obvious however, from the demonstration in the earlier stages of the meeting at St James's Hall, that the bulk of the Liberal party is not disposed to view with sympathy any one who plays the part of philosophic critic, and is reluctant to take his share in the hard every- day work of politics. It required a large amount of tact On the part of SIR HENRY CAMPBELL- BANNE RM AN to induce an important portion of the audience to appreciate the service which Lord ROSEBERY had done by his Chesterfield utterance and the much more important sequel it might have. The exposition which the Liberal leader made was at once "courteous and conciliatory," to use the terms with which Mr. PERKS described it; and seeing how often ill-advised people endeavour to sow seeds of discord between Sir Hee.ey and Lord ROSEBERY, the latter must be touched by the anxiety of the Liberal leader in the Commons to secure a better understanding of Lord ROSEBERY'S Liberalism. It is announced that the ex-Premier has consented to address a Liberal meeting in Liverpool at an early date, and the fact encour- ages the hope that he will accept the invitation whicci has been given to him so unanimously by those who are in the councils of the party. Thor would be nothing undignified in his taking a step forward after the declaration that he intended to preserve an independent line. When Lord ROSE.. EERY spoke at Chesterfield he could have no knowledge of the way in which his return to politics would be welcomed. He left no sort of doubt on the minds of his hearers, however, that in the issue before the country—on the question of confidence in the Government—he must be coun- ted with the noes. It was impossible for him to say that he would work with the Opposition until he knew whether they desired him to do so. He knew that a large section did, but we may fairly believe that he has too much regard for the old party to be willing to do anything which should further divide it and make its prospects of return to power utterly remote. Unionists will hasten to:point out that Lord ROSEBERY'S views in regard to Home Rule differ from those of the main body of the Liberal party. It would, however, be absurd in a time of national trial for those who can join hands for a definite urgent object to hesi- tate about doing so because some matter which is not at the present time within the region of practical politics will again become the question Of the hour. Lord ROSEBERY was a party to the °Die Rule Bill of Mr GfA.DSTONE. In regard to this Plank in the Liberal programme he may have modified his views, but when the time comes to again discuss it in detail, his views may again have become larger. The matter which concerns us at the present time is that the South African policy of the Government is eating into the resources of the Empire, and that in regard to its settlement the Government seems disposed to make our heritage,bitter and 005ti37.-.+T Orta ROSEBERY reprobated the language which Lord mILNER was using in reference to the finishing of the campaign and since his speech at Chesterfield the High Com- missioner has uttered a still more jarring note Lord Roseeeny distrusts the diplomacy of Mr. Oa4IIBERLAIN as affecting our relations with EuroiSean Powers. It may be remembered that the time "the he used the memorable phrase, danger is upon us," was coincident with the nego- tiations which were proceeding between Great Britain and Germany as the searching of the Eundesrath. Lord SALISBURY smoothed that difficulty, but since then the German people have become passionate in their feelings towards Mr CHAMBERLAIN and the Cabinet in which he is such a prominent figure. It does not make matters better to know that this feeling has developed largely from an exaggeration of Mr CHAMBERLAIN'S indiscreet words at Edinburgh. It is admitted that our schemes of army re-organisation are at present in a most unsatisfactory state, and Lord ROSEBERY regards their condition with anxiety. In this state of affairs Lord ROSEBERY, with his large experience, must be the first to recognise the need of a united Opposition which shall assert itself and exercise a strong influence on public

administration. His aid would be invaluable in drawing together the forces of the Opposition and in inducing the extremists of both wings to keep step. It is to be hoped that when he speaks at Liverpool he will respond to the appeal as gener- ously as it has been given him.

Rumour says that additions to the ranks of the Peerage will be fewer in future. Such a deter- mination, if indeed it has been arrived at, has not been made too soon. The House which is to be the scene of the splendid ceremonial of Thursday next has now a membership of five hundred and ninety-two, and if noble lords were to remain in fairly constant attendance would be even more in- conveniently crowded than the Lower House it- self. We are occasionally reminded that the House of Commons, with its membership of six hundred and seventy, is the most unwieldy deli- berative Assembly in the world; yet in the ordinary course of things the increase of peerages would in a few years take away this record from the Commons and give it to the Upper House. When Queen Elizabeth came to the Throne, one duke, one marquis, twelve earls, two viscounts, and twenty-seven barons sufficed, with twenty-six lords spiritual, for the whole of the kingdom—an actual total of sixty- nine. Under the Stuarts, of course, peerages began to multiply, and by the first Parliament of William and Mary the membership of the Lords had risen to one hundred and ninety-two. In the first Parliament of Queen Victoria four hundred and thirty-nine lords spiritual and temporal sat. In 1891 the number was five hundred and eleven, and the present membership (even deducting six- teen peers who are minors, and allowing for two who are both peers of the United Kingdom and representative Irish peers) is five hundred and seventy-five. Evidently the time has come for a check to the creation of peers—if, indeed, some system of English representative peers is not to be started, or a minimum to be fixed, and new barons have to wait, like most new bishops, till seats are vacated in the House by the course of time.

Is it not time that our military authorities endeavoured to obtain a ration for the British troops in South Africa which would be more digestible and sustaining, and easier to carry,than the bully-beef and biscuit to which they have been condemned during the last two years? 'Before the war the heads of the army made all sorts of costly experiments with field kitchens which were to accompany the troops and boil their coffee en route; and some culinary individual drew up a nice cookery book, with suggestions as to how to make rite pudding—rice to be soaked twenty-four hours before being boiled—and other delicacies. Mobile colums were not in the wind just then, and the War Office made the most admirable arrange- ments for comfortable picnics in the enemy's country that could bethought of. Unfortunately, war came too soon, and it has shattered all these ideals, and brought us down to the level of one day's rations, as scanty as it can be made, carried on thelhorse, or even the "couple of biscuits', of the Orange River to Bloemfontein march. The bitter experience of the past two years does not, however, appear to have taught us prudence or good sense, for no attempt seems to have been made to find a good sustaining ration which will be easily carried, and will not interfere with the freedom of the soldier's movements or put any considerable extra burden on the horse. In the Philippines, America no sooner found that she had to engage in a guerilla warfare than she cast around until she lighted on the ration she wanted —a ration which proved entirely satisfactory. England allows her troops to struggle on—at times in semi-starvation, never well fed—because her authorities do not care to search for the article they want, or because they have been ever- lastingly expecting the war to be over before it could be manufactured. It is to be hoped that Lord Roberts, who has experience in plenty on the matter, will not lose the opportunity of pro- viding for future campaigns in this respect, even if he cannot for what is left of this one.

"Johnny Briggs," the Lancashire cricketer, Is no more! No one who has followed county cricket in the past twenty years can fail to have felt sincerely sorry when they heard of his death, which occurred on Saturday. The little man was a born humorist, the comedian of the cricket field, and crowds have often roared with laughter at his acted jests, as well as given him enthusiastic cheers for his brilliant fielding and skilful work for his side. It can be truly said of Briggs that if he downed, it was not because he had no brains. To see him bowl on a difficult wicket, trying the batsman with all sorts of balls, was to recognise that he was bringing to his:work an acute intellect as well as manual skill, and he fairly won his place in representative English teams. Everyone liked him, and it is sad to think that he and George Lohmann, who were at one time the two finest bowlers we possessed, both passed away within a few weeks of each other, and both comparatively young.

It is now evident that The Poor, the Rich, and the Budget. the coming Budget will raise questions more radical and far-reaching than any financial scheme for many years past, and that, in fact, we stand at 'the present moment under the imminent threat of a revolution in our fiscal system. Sir Micaanr- HICKS-BEACH'S address to the licensed victuallers of Bristol, and his reply to kfirra of coal merchants, were couched in such careful terms that it is not possible to draw any deduction from them, except that if he can possibly let "the trade "oft lightly he will certainly do so; and that if he must come down heavily upon coal at least there will be the usual adjustments in regard to engagements already made. Cold comfort, this ! And in the meantime the tongue of rumour has been strength- ened by the open demand of Sir ROBERT Greserr and the "Times "for the replacement of burdens the gradual removal of which during the last forty years has been one of the greatest achievements of Liberal statesmanship. The only good thing we can say for; these proposals is that their character and purpose are not disguised. Even admitting that this Government of many blunders and many jobs is in a desperate position, that it is at its wits' end for money, we yet cannot but be struck by the courage of those who propose at one and the same time to lighten the taxation of the luxuries of the wealthy and to increase the taxation of the necessaries of the poor. "There should be a general recasting," writes Sir ROBERT GIEFEN, "of the framework of taxation, based upon the revival, with well-con- sidered modifications, of the indirect taxation that has been abandoned during the past thirty years and on the restoration,as far as may be possible,of the income tax to its proper position of a financial reserve." Let us see how this revolutionary appeal would work out. Between Sir Mrenexr, HicKs- BEACH, Sir ROBERT GIFFEN, and the bell-wether of the Government press, we have the fallowing suggested adjustments of taxation : To be re- lieved or passed over—lncome-tax, land values, spirit duty, beer duty, death duties. To be Taxed or Taxed more—Tea, 3d. lb. more; sugar, Id. lb. more; corn, is. quarter; timber, ils. load; petroleum, id. gallon; coal (F). Now whether " Retrenchment " be, as these financial anarchists tell us, "a belated cry," whether the principles of Liberal finance that are at once the fruit and safe- guard of the commercial supremacy into which • this country entered half-a-century ago are obsolete " or not, the evident idea of the new finance is the very ancient dodge of taxing the 1 poor in order to relieve the rich. The cartoon of 1 the inimitable " F.C.G." in this regard is highly effective. The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER is Pictured meeting a ragged urchin, crust in hand, and saying: Ha, ha ! still eating bread and treacle ? I've a good mind to stick some more on your treacle, and to get something out of your bread, too 1"

It is not only the consumer—and especially the workman's household—which is to be penalised; it is the manufacturer and trader also. This is directly seen in the cases of timber, petroleum,and coal ; but let us take the less evident case of sugar. A doubled tax, 2.e., id. per lb., means a levy of over £2 (probably £2 10s.) upon the aver- age worbingclas.s household. the effect on the citizen as consumer is therefore considerable. The 71,d. tax imposed last April is stated by the Con- fectioners' Union to have thrown several hundreds of thousands of hands out of employment, though its effect was modified by the fall in the price o sugar imports. The effect of another .3. d. will be much more serious, became there can be no such further fall in prices; and if the Brussels Confer. ence results in the abolition of continental bo un ties there will be a sharp rise, The effect on the

div.head: MATTERS OF MOMENT.
div.p: MATTERS OF MOMENT.
A Provincial Letter.

Friendly Societies have had many opportuni- ties, and generally speaking have not failed to im- prove them, for laying before the public their views on the various proposals in regard to Old Age Pen- sions. This week, however, it has been the privi- lege of the Trades Union Congress and the Co- operative Union Congress, at a joint conference in London to adopt important resolutions on the sub ject, the first of which affirms the fundi.menta necessity of any national scheme being entirely non-contributory; while another declares that any acceptable scheme must be universal in its applica- tion, and free from any attempt to discriminate betweenithe needy and the affluent,as inquiries into the character of individuals would be unsatisfactory. These may seem large orders, and we have yet to learn what leading political thinkers interested in the subject have to say of such proposals.

In some of the larger provincial towns and cities the question of Shop Clubs has occupied sonsider- able attention of late. These clubs represent a new departure in the providential movement, and the Friendly Societies are not a little alarmed that such clubs may prove inimical to their interests. In many cases, it appears, membership of the club is:made compulsory,the subscriptions beingdeducted from the wages of the members. But if these were the only objections that could be urged against shop clubs, perhaps the latter would be sub- jected to nothing worse than a little amiable criti- cism, It is alleged. however, that the shop club sets itself up in antagonism 0 the local friendly society, and that the members of the former are in many cases compelled to relinquish their connection with the latter. This is not all : for while the friendly societies are subject to registration, the, shop club enjoys perfect freedom in this respect and consequently is placed in an unduly advantag- eous position, from which it may successfully com- pete with the legitimate friendly society. It is now Etrillounced, therefore, that in the course of the ri sesee t session of Parliament a Bill will be intro- u for the purpose of effecting an equalisation of the conditions under which friendly societies and shop clubs are conducted. One of the principal clauses of the bill will insist that the shop clubs should,Public interest, be brought under a 8 stration. It is an important question stem o i n f rt ehgei and one that will no doubt give rise to much ani- mated discussion both in and out of the Parliament- ary circle.

Sir Michael Hicks-Beach. commenting on the Child Messenger Act the other day at a meeting of licensed victuallers in his own constituency, said that many members of the trade,not knowing what a sealed vessel was, had declared that they did not intend to serve children at all, and in his opinion, they could not adopt a wiser course. If the Chan- cellor of the Exchequer does not mind,it is scarcely probable that the tempsrance party Will care, if children are not served with intoxicants. Whether the parents of such children care, however, is another question. The licensed victualler, for- getting, perhaps, the fundamental truth that in this country no Government can long place itself as a shield between a particular interest and an

aroused pablic opinion, has for some days past been wondering why such a blow should have come from this particular source; while, on the other hand, the parent who had hitherto employed his child to fetch his "drop of beer,"considers that a slight has been put upon his sense of parental responsibility, as well as an embargo upon his personal liberty. The irritation thus engendered is bound for a time to be considerable. But the feeling will neither be permanent or of long continuance. The new con- ditions nave the sanction of law, and that counts for much with the average Englishman, whatever he may say or think; and they have the sanction also of an overwhelming body of public opinion,to which many of the grumblers themselves do already in their heart of hearts subscribe. He is not a bad sort of fellow, this father who sends his offspring for a pint of beer. He knows that what is done is out of consideration for the child's good, and he himself feels he would rather he on the side of the angels and have the approval of his own conscience than otherwise, though he detests being" man- , aged," or regulated by what he calls grandmotherly ' legislation,and having his duty pointed out to him. -- I The Chancellor of the Exchequer, on the occasion referred to, also stated that there might in thd Session of Parliament now entered upon, or the next, be an opportunity for effecting certain changes in connection with licensing questions, and "above all in the state of the law with regard to Clubs." In too many places, he said, the clubs were simply "bogus clubs and mere drinking places." Parliament will do wisely if it enacts cer- tain provisions by which every club in which intoxicating liquors are sold may be compelled at least to register itself as a club with certain rules, such as every well organised club ought to possess, and unless it is the intention of the Government to enact that penalties shall be imposed upon the sale of intoxicating liquors in places not so registered and regulated, Sir Michael Hicks-Beach will scarcely be justified in having directly encouraged the hope so largely indulged in and so long enter- tained not only by licensed victuallers, but by other people in every part of the provinces.

Cycling, like the poor, is manifestly destined to be ever with us. Tne last is said to have been a poor cycling Christmas, but only cyclists of s cer- tain,or uncertain calibre could expect it to be other- wise. On the wettest, the coldest, and the most stormy days they are a wheel. Hence there is much discussion in the papers as to the most suitable kind of winter outfit for cyclists. Since in season or out of it, cyclists will ride their hobby-horse, perhaps it is well that these matters should be considered. Gloves and an extra pair of stockings are said to have proved not quite satis- factory, and another suggestion is made which, though very simple, bears the imprint of reason ; namely, that in order to keep the pedal extremities warm, loose stockings and loose shoes should be worn. Those who have worn the usually tight gloves on very cold days will understand and ap- preciate the force of such advice. For the hands become so cold, owing to the proper circulation of the blood being impeded by the constricting mita- ence of the gloves, that one is frequently obliged to remove the coverings in Order to obtain relief from the intense discomfort occasioned. It IS the same with tight footgear, with the further disadvantage in this case that boots cannot be removed with the same facility,as'gloves not can the. foot be so conveniently transferred to the pocket of one's clothes as the hands. Cycling shoes are usually tight, and cants extra cold feet in cold weather. With the adoption of the suggestion referred to cycling may assuredly be randered a little less uncomfortable than it is in the winter.
RUNCORN NOTES.
[BY A CORRESPONDENT.]

Mr Naylor has again written to the Rural Coun- cil. Ills epistle was, however, received in silence. There was not even a passing comment from any- one which is rather slighting to Mr Naylor's power of expression. But it is evident that Ur Naylor does not intend to let the matter drop. He has put his hand to the plough and is not going to draw back for any person,firm, or authority. Where the Thelwall nuisance will eventually end it is im- possible to say. The only seam open for the Council and the only business-like policy to pursue is, irrespective of expense, to press for a Local Government inquiry as previously suggested. This would clear the Council from alleged lethargy, brush away the suspicion clinging to Messrs Long and Sons tannery ; and silence Mr Naylor for ever and a day.

The first pile of the Runcorn Transporter Bridge was driven in on Thursday morning. This will be welcome news to the inhabitants who are almost staking their existence on a revival of trade througft the " transporter."

The report of the Runcorn Savings Bank, pub- lished in another column, forms gratifying reading as to the saving propensities of the townsfolk. The last year has actually seen an increase in business, though, at first glance, this does not appear to be the case. I recommend readers to turn.to the ad- vertised:balance sheet for furthu details. The annual meeting, which was held late on Thursday night will be reported in our next issue.

The first meeting of the New Board was held on Tuesday evening. The meeting was not a long one —barely occupying half-an-hour—but it did more real business than the Board twelve months ago would have done in thrice the time. All the mem- bers were present. ,Needless to say the chairman and vice-c airman are now Progressives and for the next three years, it is safe to prophesy, the Board will be progressive to the back bone. The Finance Committee is now merged into the School Manage- ment Committee as it was prior to 1893 when the sectarions gained their"crowning mercy." As was remarked the Board is not a large one and the finance being a most important part of the Board's business, may as well be considered by the whole of the Board as by three members.

It is pleasing to note that the scribes are now be- ing taken into consideration. The Progressives evidently recognise that the time of reporters is equally as valuable as that of the members. The Thursday night meeting—always a bad night for pressmen—is to be abolished and the old system of holding the meetings on Tuesday is to be reverted to. The meetings will commence at 5.30 so that members and reporters will be able to have a free night. Previously the hard worked scribblers had to loiter in an ante-room waiting to ba called in to the Board's bu§iuess as committees of uncertain duration were held previous to the Board meeting. But now the " old order changeth yielding place to new." Mr Norman is deserving of the highest commendation as the prime mover in the matter.

Three years ago the Vicar in a letter to his parish- ioners said that the best thing for a sore head was a piece of sticking plaister and he seriously advised the Progressive party to patronise some pharma- ceutical establishment and purchase several lengths of this useful annihilation of soreness. Would it not be a just retribution if someone were to send him a few stips of diachvlon. Perhaps he would remember his former advice and thank the donor for his thoughtfulness. Who can tell? We live in strange times now !

The Board is fairly launched on its career, The whole tone of the speeches especially that of the Chairman is deserving of thought. It was a digni- fied utterance and mapped out the future policy of the Board. The keynote—so important to us as ratepayers was that they would not provide further school accommodation but would work their best with the materials at hand. It now remains for the Board to act up to their motto of education 1 with efficiency and economy.

One important .item leaked out at the Board of Guardians on Tuesday in the course of a desultory discussion on vaccination. The cost to ratepayers shown by the Chairman of the Finance Committee, owing to the vaccination fees becoming chargeable to the Union is really enormous. A glance at another column shows the amount that Dr McDoug- all receives from the union for vaccinating patients who are too poor to afford the cost. Quite a murmur of surprise and consternation went round. the Board when Mr Woodward read the figures out

FOOTBALL.

- -- Nearly all interest in the West Lancashire Cup Competition has evaporated in Runcorn. The Lin- nets are completely out of the running for the trophy. With the two points gained on Baturday at the expense of Wigan, Runcorn now total only six for six matches, while Warrington head the list with ten points for seven matches. Widnes are second on the list with eight points for four matches, or every point possible. If the Chemicals

div.head: maintain this form there is only one home for the { cup this season.
div.p: maintain this form there is only one home for the { cup this season.

Thematch with Wigan needs no extended com- ment. The play was as poor as the specta- tors were sparse, and these were few in , all conscience. The home players appeared to be disorganised by the absence of Houghton and Richardson, Wilkinson went back, and his place on the wing was taken by Flanagan, and the youth made a very creditable debut. lie gave promise of better things. Joseph Faulkner has served a good apprenticeship with the A team and he has been an apt pupil. His display was smart indeed. He tricked the opposing couple time after time and if he had parted with the ball more readily when he had beaten his man there would have been no room for criticism. He is a clever, plucky little player and with a little more experience ought to fully hold his own in the best company. It was a bustling, vigorous game with only a modicum of science thrown in, but Runcorn des.u,ved their victory. As the previous week Wigan had defeated Leigh by 8 points to nil they were no mean opponents.

Runcorn visit Leigh to-morrow and will be for- tunate if they do not drop a couple of points. Houghton will be away as he is a patient at Alison's Hydropathic Hospital at Manchester and will not be ready for another fortnight. Tne sloppy Leigh pitch has been the scene of many a reverse for the Runcorn team,an I Runcornians will be satis- field to drop two League points there to-morrow, if they can carry off the cup contest six weeks hence.

div.head: RUNCORN SAVINGS BANK. --- Annual Report November 21st 1900 to November 20th 1901.
div.p: RUNCORN SAVINGS BANK. --- Annual Report November 21st 1900 to November 20th 1901.

The annual meetingmf the above bank was held on Thursday evening. The following is the report given by Mr W Handley, actuary, of the b ink's business of the year. During the year the total volume of busi- ness amounted to the sum of £29,932 Os 10d, in 4080 transactions an increase in amount of £2,384 17s 8d and in numbers of 47. The amount deposited in cash was £12,886 Os 9i and withdrawals £14,285 10s ; the amount withdrawn exceeding the deposit by £1,399 103 id. This diminu- tion is accounted for by the fact that the personal deposits have shown an increase, while more than a ' corresponding sum bas been invested through the bank by depositors in the purchase of Consul stock owing to its abnormally low price, and also by more remunera- tive investments being obtainable by the depositing friendly societies on mortgage or purchase of house pen- I perty. In times of trade depression these funds remain a deposit for P considerable period with the bank, and their withdrawal usually indicates increased commercial activity, and a more general feeling of business confi- dence. A sum of £1,109 33 2d has been paid or added to accounts as interest, including stock dividends' an increase on the year of £5 21 3d. The Consul stock held for depositors shows a net increase for the year of £1,875 in nominal value. Thu number of open accounts is 1,216, as against 1,232 last year ; the amount standing to the credit of depositors being £41,536 33 = Id. Ofjthese accounts over one-fourth do not exceed an average of £5 per depositor. To meet this £41,536 3s ld the National Debt Com- missioners held £41,407 103 9d as attested by the certifi- cate a3d the treasurer as certified by him on the annual statement hell £285 53 41. These two amounts exceeded the depositors' balances by £156 13s after pro- viding the expenses of management, and increasing the balance by the sum of £l4 12381 during the year. The auditors throughout the year have kept up a continu— ous audit, and at its close subjected the accounts to a thorough examination. They have also compared a large proportion of the depositors' books with the ledger, the correctness of which t'sey vouch by their certificate appended hereto. The inspector appointed under the Savings Bank Acts has made two audits extending over Ithree days and has expressed himself as satisfied with and approving of the management of the Bank. Owiog to his removal from Runcorn Mr Had- dock is resigning his position as treasurer of the Savings Bank. El's successor, Mr F H Shaw, as the local manager of Parr's Bank is willing to accept the offioe if appointed by the trustees and managers, thus co otinu- ing the satisfactory arrangement which has existed between Parr's Bank and the Savings Bank for many years.

STOCKTON ITEiTH -PRIVATE STREET WORKS Am

The Local Government Beard wrote under date January 2cid; 1902 with reference to the application of the Council for sanction to borrow £1,140 to defray the cost of making Up Certain Streets in the parish of Stockton Heath under the Private Street Works Act 1892. The Board were advised that, in the absence of any provision in the order, constituting the parish of Stockton Heath, continuing in force in that parish the powers of the Private Street Works Act 1892 which were conferred upon the District Council by the Board's Order of the 29th October, 1895. it was very doubtful whether these powers were still in force. The Board would suggest, therefore, with the view of avoiding any difficulty in the future, that an application be made for , a fresh order conferring the powers of the Private Street Works Act in respect of the streets in question and that fresh proceedings be taken under the Act after this order has been issued. The application for the order should be accompanied by • copy of the resolution in pursuance of which it was made. The Clerk said that the Council would have to do as requested in the matter. He could not see Why the Local Goverment Board should put the matter in force again. Mr Pilling moved. " That applicst'oe b 3 made to the Local Government Board to inve it the Rural Dis- trict Council of Runcorn with the powers of the Private Street Works Act 1892 in respect of Leonard-street. Gaskell-street and Bostook-street in the contributory place of Stockton Heath." Mr Mountield seconded and tho motion was passed. SPECIAL EXPENSES.

The Local Government ti3ard forwarded copy of Order which they had issued confirming certain powers as regards the contributory places of Stockton Heath and declaring the expeoses incurred by the Council in the carrying out of those powers to be Special expenses.
_NORLEY WATER SUPPLY.

TEEL WALL NUISANCE. ANOTHER LETTER FROM MR NAYLOR.

Mr R Nayor wrote from the Rotel Great Central, London, under data January Bth as follows :—Nly London advisers desire me to press for a reply to miue of the 14% and 28th ult. Whilst lam much obliged for,and appreciate the courtesy of your formal acknow- ledgment, the business memhers of the Council will readily understand that an acknowledgement is no answer. From the report I have reczived to day I re- gret to find the tannery effluent is still very bad and your medical officer will no doubt inform you that the mere removal of solid matter therefrom will not destroy the poisonous elements. I enclose you copy of letter I am sending to the Press, and please accept this'•9 a formal communication to your Council." . .
No action was taken in the matter the letter being read without comment. _ _

Mr Reginald Potts, clerk of the Cheshire County Council, forwarded to Mr Ashton the following letter sent by the Clerk of the Grappenhall Parish Council asking what the District Council proposed doing in the construction of the sewer mentioned :—To the County Council of Cheshire.—At a meeting of the Grappenhall Parish Council information from the Clerk of toe Rural District Council showed that it was proposed to culvert a certain water course which had recently been con- verted into a main sewer for the drainage of a tannery and other property, and which had lately caused much nuisance to the inhabitant. A part of the cost of this 1 culvert is, we are informed, to be levied on the parish of Grappenball nominally aa a road improvement. We contend that this culvert is of no advantage to 1 the Parish and will not abate the nuisance but will simply move it a little farther down where it will again contaminate the neighbourhood. We earnestly beg of you to have this matter inquired into that it may be ascertained if the originators of this nusiancc cannot be made to remedy it at their own expense by proper settling tanks instead of discharging it into what has been and 6 till should be a clean water way. It would be esteemed as a favour if the Medical Officer of Health be instructed to inspect and report upon the matter before the Rural District Council proceed with the work.—S J WOODCOCK.

RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.;

The fortnightly meeting of the above authority was held on Tuesday, Mr Stokes in the chair.—Present the Rev Dr Gastaldi, Messrs A R Norman J.P„ (vice-chair- man), T Roynolds, T Wood and tne members or the Rural District Council together with Messrs G F Ashton (clerk) and W E Hough (assistant clerk).
_FRIENDLY SOCIETIES AND OUT .DOOR RELIEF.
A circular was received from itiebia-tio-naTC—o-nierence of friendly societies with reference to the provisions of the out door relief friendly societies bill.

The Clerk explained that this particular bill which the Council was asked to support by the Conference was brought before Parliament last session. At that time the Council tock no action in the matter. They again asked them to support the bill. Mr Wright proposed that the Bill should be supported If more people jained friendly societies the rates would be saved. In Halton they had one of the largest female friendly societies in England, numbering 250. Not only would each member receive so much per week but also the services of a doctor. _ .

_ Mr Norman asked how was it that they had these ap- plications then;from friendly society members. It was practically putting a premium upon applications from the members of friendly societies. _ _ _

Mr Wright explained that members getting 103 a week would not ask for relief. It was only if they got a small sum say 3s or 53. ' The Chairman : The object is, Mr Wright, that we should do all we can to encourage thritt, Mr Wright : Precisely ! Mr Norman thought that the object of friendly societies was to avoid troubling the Guardians. They had discretionary powers given to them to judge cases on their merits which was all they needed. He could not support the resolution. "fbe Chairman thought it would be well to refer the matter to the Parlimentary Committee. After further discussion the proposition was nega- tived only the mover and seconder, Mr Roylance voting for it. _ _ THE COST OF VACCINATION ON THE RATES. _ _

Mr D Davies, clerk to the Cardigan Board of Guardians forwarded a copy of a resolution passed by the Board with regard to vaccination fees and expenses, requesting the Local k Government Board to initiate such statutory roodihcatious of the Act as would enable the Guardians to re-ostablish vaccination stations so as to dispense with the necessity of domiciliary vaccination and that the Board would reduce the present schedule of fees. The support of the Runcora Board was re- quested. Mr Norman complained that the circular was not plain enough. They paid for a good many people who could afford to pay for their children to be vaccinated. They ought to do something to show the fallacy of the present. system.

Mr WooCiward said that the following facts might prove interesting while they were debating the question. The amounts paid to the public vaccinators during the past year were as follows :—ltunc:.rn district. Dr Mc Dougall,£lsl 19s;Budworth distrizt Dr Bower,£s9 13s 6d Frodsham, Dr Burton,£63 35. He had not the account for Dr Carruther's cases before him, but the total amount for the three districts already mentioned was £274 15s 6d. (Murmurs of dissatisfaction.) div.p: RUNCORN HOMING SOCIETY.

The annual general meeting of the above society was held on Friday evening. Mr W 11 Kilcross pre- sided over a good attendance :—The officers for 1902 were elected as follows :—Mr A Abel, president; ' Ur W It %Heroes, treasurer; Mr .1 Dyer. secretary ; committee: Messrs W /I Howard, R Marshall, J Heesom, W Whitby, J Dean, S Edwards, and j Dunbavin. It was resolved to send birds with the Liverpool and District Federation as usual. It 4as decided that £1 17e 6d, be given per race, 10s nor best average, and 7s 61 for the second best (both old and young birds) the old bird average to finish at Jersey, and the young birds at swiroon. The total sum to be available for prizes was £l.B 12e 6d. It was decided that the society should have a pro- duce race from Swindon. SUCCESS OF A RUNCORN MUSICIAN,

We have pleasure in announcing that the high musical honour of a fellowship of the Royal College of Organists, London, has been conferred upon Mr R Birkett Musgrove, organist of St, James Parish Church, New Brighton, and formerly organist at Frodsham Parish Church. Mr Niusgrove is a native of Runcorn, where he received his early musical training, and where he took an active part in the various musical organisations. and gave many evidences of his genius. Toe honour he has just achieved is striking testimony to his talents and his perseverance in the exacting profession be has chosen. Rnncornians will join in wishing him further successes. The annual social evening in connection with the Widrees Branches took place in Lacey-street schools on Monday evening, when there was a crowded attendaoce. Mr N E Dudley presidel,and a striking address was delivered by Mr Duncan :Mclnnes, of Lincoln. The musical portion was given by the "Cambrian Quartette " of Liverpool, who sustained their high reputation, and received an ovation on each appearance. Madame Howll and Miss Lilian Rushton al ,D p:elsel the audience immensely, while Mr F D Williams as the humorist was in great favour, bsiug encored for each item. The customary votes of thanks were accorded, and a successful evening brought to a close with the National Anthem.

Sr. EDWARD'S, RITNICoTtIq, A concert in aid of St Edward's Scoool was held on Wednesday. It consisted to a great extent of pieces given by the children of the school, opening with a" country dance" by the girls, nalf of whose number were dressed as boys in Highlau I Costume. The entertainment started well and was thorough- ly maintained to the end. The dance was encored and given again in the second part of the pro- gramme. " Mulligan's motor car," sung by one of the boys and chorused by the dancers, was thor- oughly:enjoyed. The Combination Drill,and again the Doll Drill, which was most amusing, were ex- tremely well done by the infants. " The fruit seller," was greatly admired in the excellent singing of her song for one so young, and again in the "Kilkenny cats." The recitation on the coming coronation was clearly and intelligently rendered. Mr Boraston was in his usual excellent style in the song " Out on the deep." Miss Harri- son's voice was .one of the chief charms of the even- ing and Aila 3 Kennedy gave her two songs in an excellent manner. Mr Charles Watson so much liked by the people of Runcorn enhanced -their ap- preciations of him in the songs " Marguerite " and " Terence's Farewell." It is almost needless to add since he is everywhere alike that Mr Charles Neati.s in his songs" To Rooms to Let" and "How they nurse the baby "kept the audience in roars of laughter. His more serious song "O'er the hills of 'lreland " was full of beautiful pathos, Mr T A Beckett, organist at St _Edward's Church accom- panied the artistes whilst Miss Barry and Miss Hodgson accompanied their differ- ent school children. Father Chambers in a slizzt interval thanked the artistes for their services. He also thanked the teachers for the careful train- ing for their parts, and the parents, who had gone to the trouble and expense in preparing the little ones. Lastly he thanked all present for support of the concert which must be considered int every way a success and a help to the voluntary funds of the schools.

In connection with the above Mr Walter Milling- ton on Wednesday night delivered an essay on the "Toleration Acts." There was a large attendance, Mr Simister presiding. The essayist dealt at length with the penalties which the Nonconformists once , suffered under these acts. He dilated also ' on the act of 1689, which deprived Nonconformists of religious liberty and brought to light the fact that toe Act in question still remained on the statute book, and had never yet been repealed. It would be quite possible, the essayist argued, that if extreme Churchmen or Catholics regained their ascendancy that Dissenters would again be sub- jected to the severities of the Act.—ln the discus- sion which followed, Messrs G Hayes, E Davies, II Dodd, and W A Lightfoot participated.

div.p: INTRODUCED
RUNCORN AND WIDNES TEACHERS'
ASSOCIATION.

On Saturday afternoun a meeting of the members of the above association was held at the Victoria-road , Board Schools, Runcorn, when Mr George Baddeley, of Hill Top Board School, Bursletn, and a member of the Esecutive of the National Union of Teachers, delivered an address on "Education : an ideal." There was a good attendance of members. The annual meeting of the Runcorn and Widnes Asso- ciation was held in the evening at Victoria-road schools. Mr R Des-email was in the chair, and there was a good attendance in spite of the unfavourable weather.

div.head: SECRETARY'S REPORT.
div.p: SECRETARY'S REPORT.

The Secretary (Mr George S Smith) reported that the year commenced with a membership of 32, but during the year there had been six withdrawals in consequence of removals. These had,however,been counterbalanced by the admission of nineeen new members, thus bring- ing the total membership to 95, a net increase of 13 on last year. But en ea with this satisfactory increase the committee regretted that there were still Z 3. certificated ' teachers in this district who were not members of the National Union of Teachers. Sixteen of these were lady teachers, and it was hoped that as they had for the first time in the history of the association a lady as president it would be the means of getting most of these teachers to join the local association. During the past year the following sub- jects had been discussed :—Security of Tenure, the Coekerton Judgment and its effect on Day and Evening Schools, Corporal Punishment and the Punishment Book, Representation of Teachers on Educational Com- mittees, and the Educational Bill. For the first time In the history of the association one of their members had been nominated as a candidate for the Executive of the National Union of Teachers. They hoped every mem- ber would do the best to help on the candidature of Mr J F Moulton. (Applause). The report was adopted. TUE TREASURER'S REP.)RT.

Miss L Crawford. the Lion treasurer,reported that the subscriptions from 95 members amounted to ki3 93 3d, and there was a balance in hand after the year' work- in e of £2 154. £3O 19s was forwarded to the London offices of the N.U.T., and £2 7a 61 to the Cheshire Dis- trict Union.
The report was accepted, THE N.17.T. CHARITIES•

Mr J F Moulton, secretary of the Local Board and Benevolent and Orphans Provident Society Funds, pre- sented the 9th annual report. This stated that the con- tributions from the local association to the Benevolent and Orphans Funds for the rear ended 31st December, 1901, amounted to £59 163 61, an increase of £173, 61, over last year's record. The membership of the associa- tion last year being 82 made the average subscription per member equal to 14s 7d. The total amount raised by the association since its formation now stood at £350. The committee recorded with deep regret the death of one of their members—Miss Wendt, who was for several years an earnest worker for and subscriber to these funds. Application was made through the Local Board for assistance from the funds, and a grant of £l2 was voted by the Council. This sum was duly paid to Mrs Wendt. The sincere sympathy of the mem- bers of the association WIL9 tendered to the relatives in their sad bereavement. Their cordial thanks were due to all who bad in any way assisted either by colleding or contributing to these deserving charities. In connec- tion with the association there were two life governors, ten life members, eight governors and 75 members. The report syas adoped. SECURITY OF TENURE. Mr Moulton, as Parliamentary secretary, repotted that he bad written Colonel Walker, M P. for Widnes Division, and Sir John T Brunner, Bart, M I', for the Nurthwich Division, on the question of security of ten- ure,and both members promised to give their favourable consideration to any measure which might be brought , before Parliament. THLNICS FROM THE RETIRINO PRESIDENT.
The retlini-P-re-eiden-t,-Mr R Devonied, in ;mating the chair, expressed his thanks to the members, officers and committee for their support during his term of office. - --------
THE NEW PRESIDENT.

"Miss Clayden, the new president, having taken the chair, delivered an inaugural address. Miss Clayden intimated that she would like to aim at raising the membership of the association to at least 100. (Applause.) ELECTION OF OFFICERS. The meeting then proceeded to the election of officers for the ensuing year. The following appointments were made i—Vice-president, Mr T Showan ; secretary, Mr G S Smith ; treasurer, Miss L Crawfmrd ; press correspon- dent, Mr J Brown ; secretary of Local Board and Bene- volent and Orphan Provident Society Funds, Mr J F Moulton ; Parliamentary correspondent, Northwich Division, Mr J F Moulton ; Parliamentary correspond- ent, Northwich Divison, Mr J F Moulton ; Widnes Division, Mr R Devonald ; committee, Misses Stubbs, Tyrie, Kilburn, and Messrs A Lindsay, A E Parr, and It Cookson ; representatives to conference, Misses Kilburn, Clayden, Tyrie, Hodgson, Messrs Showan, Devonald, Brown, and Moulton ; representatives to Council of the Cheshire District Union, Messrs Devonald, l S Smith, and .1 F Moulton, ex-officio.

div.head: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
div.p: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES

A WARRINGTON MAN'S CURIOUS STORY- At the Warrington Police Ceurt on Thursday. before Mr, Charles White and other magistrates. Widiam Melia, 67, Bostock-street, was charged with being found in possessio of six certs. of steel rivets which were supposed to have been stolen at 6.30 the previous morning. -The Chief Constable said he should have to ask for a remand for three days as the rivets had not been identified as the property of any particular individual or firm. Prisoner went to the works of Messrs Monks, Hall and Co., on Wednesday morning and offered six (mtg. of rivets for sale as scrap. She employee to whom he offered them said that the rivets were not scrap but were something much more valuable, most of them being worth twopence each. Information was given to the police and the man was taken into custody by P.C. Woods. When asked to account for hie possession of the rivets the man said that on the pre- vious night he was in FL publichouse and a flat man who was PI stranger to him cane to him and asked him to "stand him a drink." He (prisoner) did so and out of the fulness of his heart the flat man took him in a boat to Welton Arches and gave him the rivets as a mark of gratitude for having received the drink. In order to sift the truth or fate ehood of this statement the Chief Constable asked for a remand for three days—Prisoner was accordingly reminded until Mon- day.

div.head: MINOR OASES.
div.p: MINOR OASES.
Warrington Borough Court.

FRlDAY.—Before Mr Hepherd On the chair) Councillor John Roberts and Mr Thornton. WOMAN FINED FOR &foieULT.—Sarah Jane Ball, 7 Albert- terrace, was summoned for assaulting Mary Barton, 13 Daxin's-yard, on January 7th.—Complainant stated that she was coming home from work when defendant, after making use of foul language, struck her In the face and breast —A fine of 103 and costs was imposed. issALLE6ED ASSAULT IN A CHIP SHOP.—Herbert Houghton, 84 Laira-street, was summoned for assaulting John Naylor, 1 Stamford-street.—Mr Browne appeatred for the defendant.— Complainant stated that he was in a chip shoo to Winwick- street in company with some friends,awhen the defendant came in and commenced to usenabusive language towards him. When witness got up to go out of the shop defendant commenced to push him about and wanted to fight him. When they got to the door defendant attempted to strike him, but was prevented from doing ho by complainant's riends.—Mr Browne said the affair arose out of trade ealonsy. Houghton was formerly engaged by complainant's parents se, travelling confectioner, but seven months ago he left tteir employ and entered the service of another firm. Since then complainant had been going about to the eifferent towns at which defendant did business, telling the cus- tomers that Houghton had been near gsol three times, and consequently defendant's business had decreased. On the night in question Houghton went bats the shop and asked Naylor for andeaplanation. He denied haying assaulted complainant.—The case was dismissed. New YEAR'S DAY llPlSoDE.—Winifred Culleton, is, Old- road, was summoned for assaulting Mary McGovern, 35, Old-road. on January Ist.—Complainant alleged that defen- dant struck her a severe blow on the Iceadr with a stick,— Defendant was bound over to keep the peace and ordered to pay the costs (13s 6d.) MomDay.—Before Mr Monks (In the chair), Alderman Fran- comb, and Messrs Hayward. Wriglat and Thornton, THEFT FROM A SHOP —John Smith, 35, Town-hill, was charged with having stolen from the shop of Mr James C. Craik. Buttermarket-street, a pair of trousers of the value of ids Si at twenty reinutes'oast six on Saturday evening.—He pleaded guilty.—The Chief Constable said that the trousers were taken from inside the shop door. At the time in ques- tion Mr Craik was in the shop when he hosed a noise. seem- ingly near the doorway. He turned round and saw prisoner going away. He followed him and observed that he bat a pair of now trousers with him which were his (Mr Craik's) property, Prisoner owned to be a most unfortunate man as his movements had also been jealously eyed by PC Cooper, whO met him coming from the shop. He was stopped by the officer and taken into custody. When charged at the police station he said, " I know nothing about it.' Mr Craik did not expose goods for sale outside the shop, and the articles were well within the surveillance of his shopman. There Was no temptation to anyone dishonestly inclined,—Prisoner was Anod les and coats or in default of payment a month's Imprisonment. TnEsnicr,—Before Aldermen Shavr %rem On the eharr), and _ _

div.head: Hutchinson and Dr Fox.
div.p: Hutchinson and Dr Fox.

WANTE.D TO GO TO 0 AOL.—John Stevens, a stranger to the town, was charged with having stolen from the shop of Mr Fleming, Bridge-street, on Monday evening, a pair of boots (of the value of 4s 11d.—The Chief Constable said that Mrs Fleming, who was at the shop, missed a pair of boots from outside the door abmat six o'clock and ip.ve information to the pollee. Information of the theft was taken round to the various pawnbrokers, on a bicycle by P.C. Sankey. On arriving at the shop of Mr Houghton, Mersey-street. be saw the prisoner standing outside and another man named Itowlinson, a resident in the town, was inside offering the stolen boots for pledge. Both men were taken into custody by the officer, and the prisoner stated that FLowliason did dot know anything about the bonts,and it was at the request of prisoner that he went to pledge them. When charged Stevens said he wanted to go to gaol until the fine weather. —The Chairman : We won't give him that privilege,but we will give him a month with hard labour.

Warrington Occasional Court. THURSDAY—Before Mr P Stubbs. ALLEGED IMPUDENT THEFT AT a 01,13011 NE.—John Chad- wick was charged with stealing a man's jacket and vest, a Cotton shirt, and a case containhsg two razors and a pair of Setssors veins £l, the preperty of Arthur Mason, platelayer, 54, Bridge-street. Gioia orne. —Prosecutor stated that on De- cember 4th prisoner came to his house and asked for lodgings, stating that he was working at the Gdborne Gas Works. Witness consented to his lodging at the house. On December 13th witiaesti left home at 6.30 in the morning to go to work, leaving the prisoner at home. The articles mentioned in the Charge were inn drawer. On returning home in the evening he missed the property and also found that the prisoner had left the house. The man never returned and information was given to the police.—P.O. Sutton said he apprehended the priSotler at Mill-bank, Preston, the previous day. He was wearing the stofrn shirt. Witness took him to Wigan and charged him with the theft and he replied" Aye, its reet.”—Prisoner Was remandel for a week. Before Mr H Neild. _ .

CASE FROM ACTOZT-I:lRt—x-G;;:in-o-;nas Longshaw was charged with stealing a grey overcoat value lOs the property of Thomas Wright at Acton Grange on the 13th inst.— Evidence was given to the effect that the coat was left by the prosecutor in a Dutcb bay at Mr Thomas Ball's farm, Acton Grange on Monday and was missed the same day.— luformation was given to the pence and prisoner was arrested on the 15th lost, the coat being found in 'his house —Prisoner was remanded to Daresbury Petty Sessions.

div.p: Runcorn Petty Sessions.
MONDLT—Before Mese!' C.Reynolda (la the chair) and
J. Pritchard.

Scxr To KNITTSFORD FoR BEGGING.—Two middle aged strangers named Thomas Jordan and John Brown were sent to Knutsford for 14 days for begging in ChurCh-street on Saturday on the evidence of Sergeant Gregory. A LogiLiCloce PRISONEII.—POLICE ()BARGED WITH ASISAULT.—A stranger five feet in height.was charged at the instance of P.C. Gilpin with being drunk and disorderly an Saturday night. In reply to the usual query of " Guilty or not Guilty" prisoner replied. Guilty and I am sorry for It." The evidence showed that the man was so violent that two civilians had ti be requisitioned to bring him to the police station.—No coons, were the words uttered by the chairman Ss and cost or 14 days than the prisoner requested permission to speak. Without pausing for a reply the man excitedly and even tearfully began to tell how he bad bees awakened from a sound sleep twe hours after he had been " brought in," by two stalwart con- stables who comme.nced a meat unprovoked merciless attaek upon him. They blacked his eye and pummeled him about

the body until. he declared, his body was black and blue. He would call a doctor in who would certify that such was the case, One noliceman actually stood outside the cell door inviting his brother officers to " give it him."—The super- intendent indignantly denied the assertions of the prisoner which were without foundation.—The chairman : You can have the doctor to examine you but you must pay fis and costs or go to goal for 14 days.—Prisoner (disgustedly) " I would not pay a red cent." Sent to Knutsford accordingly. HUMSAND AND WIFE IN TROUDLE.—George Warrell Bridgewater-street, was charged with being drunk in High- street on Saturday. and his wife, Allele Warren, was charged with assaulting P.O. Gregory while in the execution at his duty.—P.C. Gregory deposed that at 10 o'clock on Saturday night he had occasion to arrest the max for being drunk and fighting with his wife.—While taking him to the station prisoner's wife ran at him and struck him on the head with a basket knocking his helmet off. She also kicked him in the ribs mid tried to atop him taking her husband, She used the most disgusting language.—Fined la and costs or 14 days hard labour. WANTED TO 03 TS GAOL.—A youth of eighteen named Edward Hargraves, a sailor, was charged with breaking a street lamp in High-street on the 11th last. From the evidence it was shown that on the night in question he was seen to pick up a stone and throw it at a gas lamp until he broke it. He then went to the police station and informed the superintendent that keying broken a lamp he wanted to be sent awey:for "fourteen days hard."—On being interro- gated by the bench prisoner replied that he had come from Liverpool and bad had his boots and money stolen from him in ql Runcorn. He had; no alternative but to walk the streets all night so he preferred to go some- where where he would be taken care of. He wanted, in fact to go to prison.—Prisoner was accordingly committed for 14 days to Knutford. COMMITTED TO THE Assizes.—Henry Caffrey, a stranger, was charged with stealing a neckerchief and a shirt.— Edward McCann, the prosecutor, stated that on the 4th January at 9 o'clock prisoner clme to his house for lodging. His wife bad gone out shopping and while he was in the,yard the man decamped with the articles produced.—P C Wilding proved apprehension of the prisoner who admitted taking the articles.—Prisoner was committed to the Assizes.

div.head: Monthly Meeting.
div.p: Monthly Meeting.
The monthlv meeting of the Warrington Trades and Labour Council was held in the Druid's Sall, Sankey- street, on Tuesday evening, Mr J Edwardson presiding over a fair attendance.
RAILWAY COMPANIES AND WORKMEN'S TRAINS.

A letter was received from the Secretary to the Lancashire Federation of Trades and Labour Councils stating that they bad received replies from the Railway Companies concerned in the memorial on Work- men's trains,which was presented in Septemberdast.The companies had consulted together, and the reply 'of one would serve for alleAtter informing the Federation that the memorial had been considered %a writer on behalf of the companies continued :—" I have to say that they have been unable to see their way to make any general reduction in the fares, or to extend the times up to which workmen are allowed to travel in the morning With reference to the request that workmen who, through stress of weather or other cause, are unable to remain at work, should be allowed to return earlier in the day, it would seem to be, the practice for such a course to be allowed en application being made. If, however, the Council will afford particulars of any cases ia which some of the earlier trains could, without inconvenience to other passengers or to the working of the trains, be made available generally for work- men's return tickets, the Railway Companies will be quite willing to give the matter con- sideration." The communication stated that this reply, although far from being as favourable as the Federation could wish, seemed to denote a desire on the pert of the companiee to meet the con- venience of the workpeople in extension of time for the return journey, and the concession to those who were unable to remain at work was of especial value. It was requested that the secretery of the Federation be informed whether there wore auy casts where liberty to return by earlier existing trains would be of sub- stantial benefit to members of the Warrington Council or to the working classes generally. The matter was left in the bends of the Secretary the opinion being expressed that Warrington workmen affiliated with the Council would not be much affected by concessions whict might be made by the companies.

THE PENRHYN CHOIR CONCERT. A Lotter wag read from the Rev F E Powell, Vicar of St. Tatnes's Church, Latchford, accepting an invitation to preside at the forthcoming cooeert to be given by the Penryhn Choir. THE PROPOSED DEMONSTRATION.

The SECRETARY read letters which had been received from a number of Trade Union leaders regretting their inability to address a Trades Union demonstration at Warrington in February. After considerable discussion it was decided to post- pone the demonstration until autumn and the members of the Council were requested to bring the matter under the notice of their societtes. This was all the business.

We had him under three doctors at different times, first trying one and then another, bat to no avail. We went on in this strain over two years, and we could see our little one gradually westing away, first in bed a week or two, tuen, if a little better, up a bit. Gifts to Poor Children.

Messrs. Unsworth,7, Lyme-street, have presented six dozes caps to boys between the ages of six and twelve years. Mr Henry Taylor, Reit., has in- structions to give tickets to that number of poor boys, with which to apply at the above address, to b,e fitted with a good cap. St. Hilda's Minstrel Troupe. The members of this troupe gave an excellent entertainment in St Hilda's Mission, Knutsford- road, on Monday evening, Part one of the pro- gramme was of an interesting character, songs, being rendered by the following :—J Grounds, W Hanson, J Shakeshaft, J Eckersley, J Pevitt, A C Lazenby, II Warburton, A. Moore, A Longstaff, and A Grounds. After the interval a clever impersona- tion of Leo Dryden as "The Miner" was given by A Moore, and the character song " One Polka," was sung in a creditable manner by A C Lazenby. 3 Booth contributed the comic song, The Handy Man," and Mr A Moore was also responsible for a stump speech entitled " Anything versus Nothing." The amusing farce, " The Mishaps of Cxsar Crum." I was heartily applauded. Mr E Davies was an effici- ent accompanist. Bold-Street Wesley Guild. A lecture entitled " Dreamland and its strange People "was given on Monday evening in connec- tion with this guild by he Rev John Gunnell. The lecture' which was b Jth interesting and instructive, opened with a few general observations on dream- land, its vast extent which includes the whole uni- verse ; its antiquity ; the splendour of its scenes its accessibility, and the personality of its people. The causes of dreams were next dealt with. The; two chief were shown to be bodily sensation at the time, and recent waking thoughts. The lecturer than dealt with the dreams of the Bible, their origin and significance; the effects of dreams ; the rapidity with which the incidents occur; and the light impression frequently left on the mind, so that the most vivid dreams were sometimes for- gotten in the morning. He said dreams were fre- quently useful—sometimes they forewarned of danger, at others solutions of difficult problems were arrived at, and beautiful music and poetry had been composed during sleep. The lecturer gave many incidents illustrating the various points in his discourse on this most fascinating and myster- ious subject. Mr J C Holland occupied the chair.

div.head: NORTHERN UNION.
div.p: THE NORTHERN UNION.
COUNTY CHAMPIONSHIP.
LANCASHIRE v. CUNIBERLAND.

At Barrow, before 6,000 spectators. The Lancashire team turned out as selected, but on,the Cumberland side Fleming appeared vice Bell In the three-quarter line. Ferguson started against a slight wind for Lancashire, and the first scrummage took place at the Cumberland twenty-five. The , Cumbrians got possession, and the ball was removed to Lancashire territory: Lancashire were penalised, and lost further ground. Whitehead got) possession from a scrum- mage, and after a fine round of exchanges Hears was collared in a dangerous position. Forward play reigned for a time, and Leee made a fine save from the Lancastrians. This was followed by a tine sprint on the part of James to the Cumberland Rms.-and after some faulty work by the Lanca- shire backs James threw out to Wilson, and he galloped over and scored near the corner. W James made a fine but fruit. less shot at goal. Lancashire were now showing to better advantage, and W James was prominent. They were again penalised however, and Kitchen landed a goal, which the referee disallowed foe offside. Hostilities were now in the centre. Fish kicked finely to the Cumberland twenty- five James again passed out to his right, and a nice oppor- tunity was spoiled by a faulty pass. Lancashire, by credit- able footwork, Invaded once more. and, Cumberland being penalised, W James brought off a brilliant goal. The Cum brians now forced matters, and gradually worked up the field. Whitehead was smart outside the pack, and, getting possession, gave to Fletcher, who transferred to Hears at the right moment, and he scored at the corner. Kitchen failed at the kick. Lancashire now livened up, and after exciting work in the Cumberland territory one of the finest move- ments of the day culminated in Hogg scoring a brilliant try. The ball was passed from man to man, from left to right of the tlfield. W James failed at the kick, The Cumber- land defense now appeared broken, and Lancashire,keeping tip the pressure. W James added another. Preston mis..ed his kick. Half-time :—Lanoashire, one goal and three tries (11 points) ; Cumberland. one try (three points). Atkinson restarted. S James got hold in the Cumberland half, and by a tricky movement eluded all except the full back when he passed, but the ball subsequently went for- ward. In the next moment Fish was brought down in a good position. Treweek tackled Leek, and put Lancashire in s fine position. Poor passing spoiled the chance, however, and the Cumbrians went away with a dangerous rush,which Thomas saved in' splendid style. From the ensuing scrum- mage Jones passed out to his backs, and after brilliant work Hogg ran over and added the fourth try. W James failed at goal. 8 James ran finely, but a pass forward spoiled. Still attacking, W James kicked a penalty goat. From a long kick by Thomas tie ball went dead, After a fine round of passing, in which nearly all tie backs took part' Hogg scored. W James failed to improve. Cumberland reaohed the Lancashire line, which Fletcher creased, but the ball had then passed forward. Lancashire had the best of matters to the finish. Result :—Laneashire. two goals and eve tries (19 points) ; Cumberland, one try (three points). The following were the teams : Lancashire.—R L Ilionaas (Oldham), tack; A Hogg and R Wilson (Broughton Rangers), captain, G Dickenson and Fish (Warrington), threequarter backs ; W James and S , James (Breugiston Etaagers), half backs ; J Ferguson (Old- ham), P Tourney (Salford), G Wilkinson (Oldham), J Rhapps (Salford), J Harrieon (Rochdale Hornets) J Preston (Swin- ton), F Treeweek (Barrow), and J Ruddick (Broughton Rangers), forwards. Cumberland.—J Pattinson (Aspetria), baek ; 3 W Hears and T Fletcher (Seaton), Fleming, and W Kitchen (l/udder- s/old and Wath Brow). tbreequarter backs ; J Whitehead (captain) and 3 Leek (Hillom), half backs ; J Lazenby and A Humberson (Aspatria). J Owen and II Tinnion (Seaton), J. Beetham and J. Atkinson (Slillone). J Grimes (Wath Brow), and 11.1 Westmorland t' Whitehaven Reereation). forwards.

div.head: NORTHERN LEAGUE.
div.p: THE NORTHERN LEAGUE.
WARRINOTON'S SD FATE.

- ----- It was Warrington's misfortune to take the field on Satur- day minus seven of their best men, two of whom, Dicken- son and Fish, were playing for Lancashire at Barrow; The other absentees were Hallam, Burgess, Morrison, Fell, and Ashton, while Jones, the first reserve, was also unfit. War- rington were thus weakly represented, while Halifax had a good team, Jack Riley and Kitson (forwards) being the only absentees. The w,atber was damp, but there would be a crowd of about 4,000 present when operations commenced. Mr Marshal!, of Bradford, was the referee, and the teams lined out as follows
Halifax : Little, full back ; Nichol', Rfgg, Joe Riley and Maßison. throeguarters ; Morbsy and Brown, half-backs ; Bartle, Morton, Hammond, Swinbank, Bula.er, Winskiil, Heap and Ma Hinson. forwards.

Warrington : Ratcliffe, full back; Foster, Hookenball. Isherwood and Harris, threequarterS ;H Bate and Allen, half-baoks ; Boardman, Eden, Edmondson, Taylor, J Swift, W Sv;ift, Dakin and *Boos. forwards.

Warrington started against the breeze,and Foster mulling the catch from the return, Ratcliffe was early tested but cleared well. Isherwood got hold and ran splendidly into Halifax quarters, the home team taking up the attack. Folder ran close up to the line where Warrington seemed to have a chance but Hockenhell was not np. Isherwoed was prominent but the half-back play on the home side was poor, both Bate and Allen being slow. Warrington kept the ball in the visitors 'quarter, and a touch kick by Allen landed under the posts where Rlgg safely marked. Harris made a vigorous dash on the right wing but was brought down. The visitors next had a turn on the attack, and aided by strong kicking from Little they got down to the home line, where Bartle nearly scored. Halifax passed across but gained no ground and Warrington got back te centre. Hockenhall grassing Little Scrambling play followed Foster and Nicholl almost break- ing through for their respective sides. Halifax got down again and the forwards handling the ball smartly, Bartle scored near the posts, Little raissing the goal. Warrington rushed to the other end again, the forwards dribbling to Little who was lucky to save. Bo trdman and Whaskill came to blows and both received marching orders. Halifax attacked again and Morley was held near the line. The , borne team expected the whistle to go and Morley after I struggling parted to Rigg who walked over amid howls from the crowd. Little again failed at goal and at half time Halifax led by 2 tries to nil. Little resumed and the home team at once dashed down to the Halifax end. Harris carne in for a caution, and the referee's actions were generally disapproved of. Give and take play followed, and from a lialifax attack Nicholl nearly got in at the corner. Ratc:iffe tackling well, Warrington made a spurt and Hockenhall and Foster got clear away. They ran down to the full back and then Foster knocked on with a certain try at his mercy. This about extinguished Warrington's chanees,though they attacked again before the close and Isherwood dropped a goat. Final : Halifax 2 tree (6 points): (Warrington I goal (2 points). LEIGH V. BROUGHTON RANGERS. About 4,000 spectators witnessed this return match at Leigh. Leigh commenced with great dash and forced their way into the Rangers' quarter, and quick passing enabled Towers to score a grand try three minutes from the start. Molyneux placing a goal. • Play was even after this, but bad mulling on the part of the Leigh three-quarters gave the Rangers a chance, and the forwards dribbled over the line in a body for Woodhead to score, Orem falling at goal. Leigh attacked vigoroutly after this reverse, but keen tackling pre- vented them scoring, and after some exchange kiceing Harry , broke (+lean away and transferred to Wlddeeon, who raced away from his opponents and scored near the corner, the place kick failing. At the interval the Rangers led by six points to five. Rain fell heavily in the second half. but nevertheless both sides fielded the ball well. Each attacked in turn, but for a time the defeneelwas invulnerable, Towers had a good chance of placing a penalty goal for Leigh, but failed, and then after aceurate wide passing by the Rangers' backs Hampson got over at the corner, no goal resulting. Leigh worked very hard to score, but found rielding a great stuntbling block, and the Rangers eventually won by three tries (nine points) to a goal and a try (five points). SWleroer V. BRIGHOUSE RANGERS. This return match was played on the Swinton ground, and considering the state of the weather, there was a good num- ber of spectators present. From start to finish Brighouse were completely overplayed, and they offered such a feeble
111 E EXAMINER FRIThiY, JANUARY 17 1902

resistance to the Swinton attack that the game had lost all its interest when the interval arrived. A very one-sided game ended :—Swinton, three goals and nine tries (33 points) ; Brighouse Rangers, nothing.
-OLDEaIf V. iLIJALET.

These teams met at Watersheddinge before 6,000 speota- tors. The second quarter of the garas was very text. Spottis- woods scoring three tries In quick succession. Civil in each case being mainly responsible for the success by beating the Opposing backs and passing to the wing man. Dixon kicked two goals. After the interval the visitors played a more vigorous game and attacked strongly at Owes. but failed to get through, Mitchell twice dropped at goal without sue. cess, The Hunslet defence vras much more stubborn and sound in the second half, and it was just in the last two or three minutes of the game when Civil Booted behind the , posts after a capital passing run between himself and Spottis- woode. Dixon added another goal making the final score— Oldham, three goals and four tries (18 points) ; thanslet.
HUDDERSFIELD V HULL,

Sutcliffe started this game at Hudd'ersflelcl. Trowell returned, and Marsden. Dewburst and Larard executed a tine movement, which culminated in Deere scoring from a pass by Dewhurst, Sutliffe failing at goal. After the restart Marsden missed a chAnce : Ritmo dribbled from half-way and scored, Jacques converting. Play continued fast, and Dewhurst scored, Larard failing. Huddersfield kept up the pressure, Larard scoring again, and himself converted Wimpenny also got over before half-time, at which stage the score Wall —Huddersfield, one goal and four tries (14 points), Hull. one goal and one try (five points). After the interval Parkinson restarted, and the Hull backs .were at once prominent. Townend beingsstopped just outside. The Huddersfield forwards, led by Sutcliffe dribbled clear, and Wimpenny was nearly in. Play continued fast, both ends being visited in turn, Dewhurst, Larard, and Walter Dew- hurst passed well, the latter scoring, Driver missing the place. Hanahrecht made a good run, but lacked support and the final score was :—Huddersfield, one goal and four tries (17 points) ; Hull, two goals and one try (seven points).

div.head: SOUTH-WEST LANCASHIRE LEAGUE. RUNCORN v. WIGAN.
div.p: SOUTH-WEST LANCASHIRE LEAGUE. RUNCORN v. WIGAN.

At Runcorn on Saturday. The ground was wet and heavy The visitors started,and alter the opening movements Wigan dribbled the ball over the line, and Webster scored. Nelson kicked a goal. Some fluctuating play followed, the game being contested in midfield. Runcorn carried hostilities to the Wigan 25, and Moulton made a futile kick at goal. A minute later Moran scored for Runcorn at the corner,Mounon again failing at goal. A series of exchange kicks saw the ball find touch. Runcorn got a footing ia the Wigan 25. and after tight scrimmaging Butterworth dropped a splendid goal. The game became more exciting from this, and Wigan made vigorous efforts to score. Nelson failed at goat from a mark. Shortly afterwards half-time was called, with the score :—Runcorn, 5 points; Wigan, 5 points. Farmer restarted, and at once the Greens became aggres- sive, but their efforts to score lacked method and cohesion. The Wigan backs, Rothwell, Nelson and Webster essayed a passing movement, but it broke down and then bath sides indulged in some fine kicking, and Joseph Faulkner cleverly bluffed his opponents to put Runcorn on the attack bat goo kicking by Roose and Nelson drove them back. Jolley and Faulkner gained much ground, Nelsoa broke splendidly away and started a movement, but Roose was well tackled. A passing bout took Runcorn close to the Wigan line and Farmer scored. Moulton failed at goal. The game veered about after this and Wigan once reached the Ituncor n line. hut were driven out. Final :—Runcorn, one goal 2 tries ; Wigan, one goal one try.
