Warrington twice missed dropping goals by narrow shaves. Half-time :—Rochdale Hornets "A." nothing ; Warrington " A," nothing. Following a run ;by Turner,Hickey placed another goal. Turner scored from a long pass by Rckersley. Hickey again adding the extra points. Leech also scored for Rochdale. Result : Rochdale Hornets, eight points ; Warrington, nil.

WIDNEB " A " V RUNCORN " it."

At Widnes on Saturday, in wretched weather, on a heavy miry ground, and before a poor gate. Runcorn started and at once rushed down into the home quarters with a vigour that gave much promise, The home custodian bad to kick dead, but this relieved matters, and a fine dribble half the length of the field by Lomas enabled Leyshon to get by Furnival and to pub down. No improvement followed, but the home team kept up the attack and before very long a fine piece of combined work by Rispan and Bown enabled the former to place a very nice second try under the posts,Taylor making the needful addition of points. Widnes continued to press up to the interval. Half-time: Widnes, eight points; Runcorn, nil, The restart still saw the Widnes men making good headway and a fine breakaway forced Furnival to kick beyond, A splendid piece of work was witnessed on the part of Barber, who received in a difficult position trickily elected half a dozen opponents and then gave to Lee who had a clear run over. The additional points were not added, but soon another big rush again saw Widnes over the line, half a dozen of the homesters doing the part of escort to the oval. Again there Was no improvement. At this staze Peters was injured and had to be carried off the field. On the resumption Flown got the ball to his feet aud kicked across to McCarthy who scored, Webster failing at the place. Final: Widnes " A," 17 points : Runcorn "A," nil.

BOUTHPoRT CENTRAL V WARRINGTON. Owing to the late arrival of Warrington this match at bouthport on Saturday started a quarter of an hour behind time. Central were still short of Shadbolt, but Sinclair, the popular half back, tarried out for the first time after his illness, and met with a warm reception from the kick-off. Central attacked and Gibson shot wide. Central had most of the Play, but Hobin kept goal in grand style for the viii- tori. A dash which Kelly made along the line saw him wrongly awarded in touch. Harrison proved himself the Oak of the Warrington forwards at this stage, but shot badly. Central easily maintained their advantage, but It was some time before they scored their first goal, though Cooper just previously had a brilliant shot saved by Hobin. It was Atherton who scored by a well-saved corner by Kelly. Then Cooper placed the homesters further ahead by a clever effort. A moment later Lang had a goal disallowed for off-side. Half-time was blown at the end of forty minutes. Half- time: Southport Central, two goals ; Warrington, nil. Central had only ten men in the second half. Sinclair not reappearing. Gibson scored Central's third goal, and Ather- ton added a fourth. Conner ores hurt, and was carried off I the field, leaving Southport with only nine men. div.head: LECTURE IN THE MASONIC HALL, WARRINGTON.
div.p: LECTURE IN THE MASONIC HALL, WARRINGTON.

The fourth meeting of the session of the War- rington Literary and Philosophical Society was held on Monday evening. The President (Sir J D Buckton) occupied the chair. Mr R Stockdale. M.A., of Leeds, greed a paper on " Weather and Weather Forecasts," illustrated with slides, the lantern being carefully manipulated by Mr Parkin- son. Mr Stockdale contended that the fact that we" had no climate, but only samples of weather," might be put down to our geographical position in the North Atlantic, coupled with our insular condi- tion. He referred to some of the , instruments by means of which observations as to the weather were made, the most important being the barome- ter, which really meant " a weight measurer." It weighed the atmosphere, and co he of service it must be accurately made. Theta was another kind of barometer known as an aneroid, which could be made very sensitive. The principle of this was the pressure of the atmosphere which acted on a par- tially exhausted steel box. The variations of the pressure pressed in or allowed to expand the upper part of the box: That movement was communi- cated to a spring and to other parts of tee mechan- ism which actuated a pointer travelling over a dial. These instruments were very sensitive, but their indications ought occasionally to be com- pared with those of a mercurial barometer which must be considered the more accurate' The lecturer gave descriptions of the thermometer and anemometer and also described the system of taking observations at the Meteorological stations. Referring to cyclones, the lecturer painted out that the weather accompanying a cyclone was of the storm order. Allusion was also made to the phenomena of thunderstorms. He pointed out that when gales were expected ports were warned, and signals hoisted called the north and south cones (of which diagrams were shown), many accidents and loss of life being averted.—A short discussion fol- lowed which was briefly introduced by the Presi- dent.—Mr May,in proposing a vote of thanks to Mr Stockdale, said he hoped the lecturer's idea of being able to obtain by means of wireless telegraphy from ships at sea proper signals as to the weather might be realized.—Captain Appleton seconded, and re- marked that it had often been said that there were few men who understood all there was in the daily newspaper ;in fact,he questioned whether there was any man who could explain everything in the " Times," At all events the lecturer had taught them something about one part of the " Times," namely, the weather chart. Now he should always read his paper with additional interest. The Cap- tain alluded to his experiences of thunderstorms in I South Africa. On one occasion they were in an ex- posed position on one of the high kopjes and from four to five o'clock every night they regularly expected a violent thunderstorm, and the storm generally seemed to follow the path of the river. The lightning looked very beautiful behind the large clouds at night, and they used to spend a long time watching it. On another occasion, while on a mountain 6,000 ft. up, he had a sentry on duty on a pitch dark night. He could not see the man, but a light was playing about the point of the bayonet. The sentry did not like it and he (the speaker) told him to return his bayonet.—Ht S Kenyon asked whether the weather was affected by the moon, and what was the cause of the :constantimet witals in the spring. Were they caused by icebergs 2—The resolution of thanks was then put to the meeting and carried.-51r Stockdale, in reply, remarked that the thunder- storms in South Africa were particularly brilliant, but they could not reduce them to anything like a law. They often followed up the valley and kept to the course of the stream more or less, He did not think there was any explanation to be given why they did so. With reference to tale remark about the bayonet, there was no doubt that it was acting as a sort of lightning conductor, and it was, therefore, advisable that the sentry should put it down. Pietermaritzburg at one time was infested with thunderstorms, but by supplying the town with a considerable number of lightning conduc- tors the inhabitants got rid -of the storms alto- gether. With regard to the cold winds in spring he did net think there was any explanation, although the probability was that the north-east winds had come from places whew there were ice- bergs. A question had been asked about the weather and the moon. Strange to say, as he was on his way to the meeting that evening a friend said to him, "The moon is on its back ; we shall have some rough weather." (Laughter.) He did not tell him it was all moonshine, but there was a certain amount of folk-lore about the matter. (Laughter.)

div.head: CAN DEAFNESS BE PERMANENTLY
div.p: CAN DEAFNESS BE PERMANENTLY
CURED?

A late issue of the " Journal for the Deaf" contains the reports of a great number of cases illustrating the permanency of the cures effected by the Drouet treat- ment, a method of administering special medication for the ears that is attracting widespread attention. So marked, in fact, is the success of this specialised treat- ment that the Editor of the " Journal for the Deaf "is now publishing the monthly records of the Drouet In- stitute as a '• Supplement." In the " Supplement" for December we note especially the case of the Rev. Heel, who suffsred for 30 years from deafness accompanied by the most intolerable noise,: in the head. On several occasions the Rev. Mr. Heel attended specialists, but with no iiisfactory remit. Having heard repeatedly of the favnrable results obtained by the Drouot treat- ment he decided to try once more,and was surprised by the complete restoration of his bearing. That his cure was !absolutely permanent is showed by the follow- ing :
47, Chetwynd-road, Dartmouth Park. London, Dec. 5, 1001.

Dear Sir,—My hearing continues satisfactory up to the present time. Noises in the head never trouble me et all. I can testify to the fact that I am well satie- fied with the reat benefit derived from the Drouet Treatment.—Yours

(Revd.) W. HEEL. P.R.—This letter contains a faithful account of my experiences:since my care three and a half years ago. Those who are interested in Deafness or disease ot the ear, nage, or threat will find in the " Journal for the Deaf" a description of upwards of 200 cases recently cured by the Droupt treatment. A free copy of this journal can be obtained by post on application to the secretary, Regent'a-park-rocd, London, N.W. The journal is accompanied by a Pathological Report Form which enables each patient to describe his case clearly. Any advice by correspondence is absolutely free, as are also the consultations by means of the Report Form.

div.head: PADGATE.
div.p: PADGATE.

CHILDREN'S TEA PARTY.—The anntnl tea party and entertainment given to the children attending the Wesleyan Sunday school was held last Friday in the Wesleyan School. Tea was served at 4 p.m. to about 230 scholars, after which the children played games and indulged in a good romp until seven o'clock, when the entertainment began. The chair was occupied by Mr Frank Harris, who spoke a few appropriate words to the children. The programme was then proceeded with and consisted of a pianoforte duet, songs, recitations, dialogues, scarf drill and several action songs. A sailor's hornpipe, which was danz..ed by a little boy named Harry Ward, six years of age, was excellently performed ; his costume also being appropriate. During an interval the medal, which had been gained by scholars who had shown zeal in helping forward the "Twentieth Century Fund," were distributed by Miss Bennett and Mrs Thornton. Altogether the very creditable number of 120 were awarded to the Padgate Children, At the conclusion of the concert, the Chairman presented the prizss which had been gained by regniar and punctual attendance. They numbered 75 and comprised some very pretty and useful books. After a vote of thanks had been accorded to the Chairman, the Doxology and "God save the Bing" were sung and the proceedings concluded, each child on leaving the school being presented with an orange.

The Dartmouth trawler Orlando,reported at Penzance on Wednesday afternoon, and the trawler Latonie, were run down in the Channel the same day by the steamship Toftwood. The Toftwood proceeded to Cardiff with a boy named Harris, the only survivor of the Latonia's crew of four,

On Wednesday, a young man named Robert Lewis, employed at the Horsehay Ironworks, near Wellington Salop, fell off some iron girders into a tank of petroleum and by some means the petroleum became ignited. The unfortunate man was burnt in a shocking manner before he was rrscued. L,lrd Lansdowne entered upon his fifty-third year. on Wednesday. The dates in his official life are:—Under Secretary for War, 1872-4; Under-Secretary for India Office, 1880 Governor-General of Canada, 1883-8 ; Viceroy of Indis,lBB9 93 ; Secretary of State for War, 1895-1900; and Secretary for Foreign Affairs since 1900 The Central Nowa announces that the telegraph wires leased by the Column Printing Syndicate have been maliciously damaged in London with a view to prevent the recording machines of tho company from working correctly, and that on December 17 a piece of wire was found to have been maliziously fixed and connected with the Column Printer wire crossing Fleet-str-et. A reward of £lOO is offered for such evidence as shall con- , vict the perpetrator.

div.head: "A LIFE'S REVENGE."
div.p: "A LIFE'S REVENGE."
Judgment in the Warrington Theatrical Case. Interesting Evidence.

At the Warrington County Court on Saturday, his Honeur, Judge Bowen Rowlands, K.C., cencluded his bearing of the action in which Anna de Gray, an actress sought to recover £5O damages from Marie Dagmar, proprietress of "A Life's Revenge" Centpany for per- sonal injuries. A counter-claim had been issued by the defendant for £5 for money lent, but at the first bear- ing it was agreed that £5 was due to the defendant from the plaintiff, less five days' wages amounting to I£2 is Bd.—Mr A. Browne conducted the plaintiff's case andltdr. Glever of Sinethwick,represented the.defendant. Plaintiff'd case, as stated by Mr Browne at the fizst hearing, was that she was engaged to take the part of Ottercia Vittoria (a Red Angel) in " A Life's Revenge." a play which was presented at the Royal Court Theatre, Warrington,during the week commeccing September 30. The chief scene was one in which plaintiff and Miss Dagmar fought a duel with swords. On the first night the duel passed off so well that the performers were recalled. Oa Tuesday night for some reason or other that they could not Sod out or imagine, the duel was a terrible affair. In the fight Miss Dagmar had to disarm the plaintiff, throw away her sword, take hold of the plaintiff by the throat and force her to her knees. On Tuesdsy night, instead of doing this, it was alleged that Miss Dagmar not only forced plaintiff to her knees, but pushed her head back until it touched the stage behind her. Plaintiff called out " You are hurting me," but defendant took no notice and continued to shake her. Sae isubsequently dragged plaintiff to her feet, and threw her forward, causisg her to fall on the stage. Plaintiff felt very great pain internally, but she managed to get up again and resume her sword. She was, however, unable to continue the duel, as " everything around her was swimming." and she at length threw down her sword and fell on the stage. The curtain was rung down, and there was uproarious applause, as the people thought it was good acting, whereas it was acting in reality. The audience accorded a recall, but defendant refused to go on the stage with plaintiff. Plaintiff was taken to her dressing room, but ultimately resumed her performance. She suffered great pain during the night, but she again went through the due/ scene on Wednes- day. That night nothing exteaordiaary occurred, and plaintiff was complimented on her acting by Miss Dag- mar, Plaintiff also played on Thursday and Friday evenings, but on Saturday she was taken ilaand:Dr Pea- cock° had to be called in. Plaintiff was ill for a fort- night, and had suffered great agony.—Plaintiff gave evidence in support of this statement, and in cross-ex- amination denied that on Monday,Tuesday. Wednesday,, and Thursday evenings her fighting was " very feebly' done." She was not " fighting the air." She did not complain to the stage manager of the affair.—Henry Stoughton, a property man at the theatre and Dr Pea- neck° gave evidence in support of plaintiff's case. Oa Saturday the case for the defence was heard. At the outset Mr Glover addressed the court, and said the case was one of very great importance to his client. perhaps even of mere importance than it was to the plaintiff herself. Miss Dagmar had /been in the theatri- eel profession all her life and had been manageress of a company for 12 or 13 years. It Was of vital importance that her good character before the public should be maintained. If she lost this case a stigma would attach to her for life. The plaintiff did not stand to lose any- thing except the money. With the defendant it was not a question of money, but a question of honour. Plaintiff said that his clieet committed a brutal assault upon her, an almost more than aggravated assault. It had struck him as being strange that no complaint was made at the time by the plaintiff. Mr Browne said the whole of the members of the com- pany came down and commiserated with her. His Honour said be had it on his notes that she did not complain to the stage manager or the manager on the Tuesday, but to Miss Dagmar on the Wednesday. Mr Glover proceeded to criticise the evi- dence of the plaintiff and her witnesses. He deliberately said that the plaintiff had concocted this case, and was a very clever actress. The witness Houghton corroborated the plaintiff with regard to the duel scene. It would be for his Honour to determine how far he was drawing upon his imagine- tiers. Ho said at the last hearing that !lee had no interest in the case, but he (Mr Glover) found he was tie very man to introduce Miss de Gray and Miss Ault another member of the company to Mrs Williams, the landlady who was a relation of his. Be (Mr Glover) thought, therefore.ehe had some interest in the case. , Turning, to the alleged aseault, he said he would call ' medical evidence to the effect that it would ba ve been physically impossible for plaintiff to have been pushed hack as described without susttiniug a rupture. No undue violence was used by the defendant on this Tuesday night. The duel Was fought very poorly by the plaintiff from beginning to end every evening, and it was such a poor show that Miss Dagmar was obliged to give plaintiff notice on Wednesday. Plaintiff did not seek to shew any motive for the alleged violence and he (Mr. Glover) asked if it were possible that his client would for the firs time in her life let her temper get the better of her and do something which she bad no reason for doing. Defendant and all the witnesses would tell his Honour that no undue violence was used by the defendant at any time and on Tuesday the fight was not out of the ordinary. During plaintiff's connection with the company, defendant had really acted the part of the good Samaritan and lent her money Marie Dagmar, the defendant, gave evidence bearing out this statement. She said that whilst she had been a member of the company plaintiff had received nothing but kindness from her. On the Tuesday evening in question witness did not use any violence towards plaintiff and Miss de Gray did not complain of being hurt. On Wednesday evening plaintiff made the re- mark that "She was afraid she was very stupid in the duel." In cross-examination defendant denied that she had ever injured another person who took plaintiff's part. Miss Pereira had played in the part before plain- tiff. She had not inured her internally and ehe did not leave for that reason. At this point Mr Browns produced a letter which he said had been voluntarily written by Miss Pereira, but his Honour refused to accept it as evidence. Defendant was allowed to read the letter and after doing so she said she had never injured Miss Pereira in the duel or anyone else who had taken part in it. Several witnesses were called, principally members of the defendant's company, who stated that nothing ua- usual occurred on the Tuesday evening. Keine. Thorpe, dressmaker, Batley said the plaintiff when at Batley complained to her of pains in her side. Marie Ault, who occupied the same apartment as the plaintiff said Miss de Gray never made any com- plaint to her about Miss Dagmar. Witness bad never heard any previous complaint against the defendant. She knew that a doctor was called in to attend the plaintiff but she thought plaintiff was suffering from pains in her side. Dr Haynes, of Birmingham, said the plaintiff's in- jures would in his opinion have been more serious if what had been described took place. Be did not think t she would have been able to take any further part in the performance on Tuesday night or on Wednesday, Thursday and Friday nightie—Cross-examieed : The doctor attending the patient had a better chance of giving an opinion than he had. His Honour, in giving judgment, said be thought the issue of the ease was of more importance to the plain- tiff than to the defendant, because loss of temper, if such it was, seemed to him to impose much less moral obliquity than, as had been said it was, deliberate framing and bringing of a concocted action supported by flagrant and wilful perjury. Plaintiff might be mis- taken iti attributing b defendant expressions which she thought she heard. It might be that she had exaggera- ted the position in which her head was placed. The fact remained that whereas she went on the stage in her nor- mal condition she went off in a very different state altogether. That was prove a beyond con- troversy. Houghton was an absolutely indepen- dent witness. If he was prejudiced at all he was prejudiced in favour oh Mrs Williams. Those witnesses of the defendant's who were members of the company could not be said to be less interested than a person who recommended plaintiff to lodgings. Defendant said Miss de Gray made no complaint. Miss do Gray swore she did. She said she told Miss Dag mar that she was hurting her. She complained to Mrs William. Miss Ault, he did not suggest anything against her, had done her best to support defendant's case, but in the light of the cross-examination of Mr Browne he could not say that either she or any of the other witnesses for the defence had been very successful. He was quite willing to accept Miss Dagmar's state- ment that she did not lose her temper, but it was diffi- cult to reconcile absolute equanimity with the very sudden notice whieh she gave to a person who was aic. proving every night." It might have been uninten- tional negligence on her part in applying force which should not have been applied ; but for the consequence of it she was liable. He saw no reason to abates single jot of the claim. It seemed to him to be extremely moderate,and he gave judgment for the plaintiff on the claim for £5O and costs and for the defendant on the counter-claim for £2 18s 4cl without costs. Mr Browne asid that as the case was one effec. ng the profession be would ask for a certificate authorizing extra costs to be allowed. His Honour said it was a case of common negligence. The case was only Of importance to the parties con- cerned. It did not affect any question of theatrical discipline and he could not grant the certificate.
Donation to the Nursing Association.

The sum of £3O has been recently given by the Order of Druids (Warrington District) as a grant te the funds of the Warrington District Nursing Association. This generous action on the part of the membel of the Order is worthy of every COM- mendation.

div.head: WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.
div.p: WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.
Interesting Cases.

TIIURSDAY.—Before his Honour Judge Bowen Rowlands H.C. AN EX-FOOTBALLER'S CLAlM.—William Dillon. " Raven Hotel," Fennel-street, claimed £5 from Howarth Marsh, Granby-street, Liverpool, which he alleged he lent to the defendant who had not repaid it.—Mr Unsworth appeared for the plaintiff and the defendant was represented by Mr Layton. barrister, of Liverpool,—Mr Unswortb said the plaintiff was very well known in Warrington having been captain of the local football team and played for his county. On the 30th March, 1931, defendant came into his house in company with a gentleman named Robert Fleming. Mr Foaming introduced defendant to Mr Dillon as "Mr Marsh. of Liverpool, my family butcher." He added "I want to know whether you would mina lending him £5." Plaintiff at once replied "Certainly Mr. Fleming if he is a friend of yours." Plaintiff put his hand into his pocket, produced the £5 and love it to the defendant. Unfortunately about six weeks afterwards Mr Fleming died very suddenly. About a month later, Mr. Dillon made II inquiries aslto the address of the defendant, and having obtained it from a brother of the late Mr. Fleming he wrote two letters and received no reply. He then went to see defendant at Liverpool, and defendant told him that he did I not lend the money to him but to Mr. Fleming.—The defence was that Mr. Fleming borrowed the money from the [ plaintiff and then lent defendant £5. The money was [ repaid to Mr Fleming.—After hearing the evidence of defen- dant and his brother, his Honour said the case was an absolutely undefended one. He did not believe a word that defendant or his witness had spoken. He would give judg- ment for the plaintiff for the full amount with costs. SEQUEL TO AN ACCIDENT AT Whim= AsYLUOl.—ldichael Nevin, labourer, of 9 Appleton-street, Warrington. claimed £25 from Messrs Robert Neill and Sons. cantracters, Man- chester, for damages for personal injuries caused on the 7th of October, whilst a workman in the employ of John Evans, a sub contractor to the defendants at-Winwick Asylum, by a fall from a defective way" or platform erected by the defendants at Winwick Asylum—Mr A Browne represented I the plaintiff ; Mr 1 ipping, barrister, appeared for the defendants, mad Mr Adshead Elliott barrister. appeared , for a third party (John Evans). Mr Browne, in stating the case for the plaintiff, said his client Was in the employ of John Evans, who was a sub-contractor under Messrs Neill and Sons, for the plastering at the new asylum at Wlnwick. The plasterers had to get on with the work before the floors were put in. The foreman plasterer (Mr Agnew) asked Mr Robinson, the foreman for Messrs , Neill, to put in the joists in the corridor so that the plasterers could rest a platform upon them. The joists were not put in and the result was that are plaintiff had to carry all his stuff for the plasterers up a narrow plank, seven Inches wide. Whilst returning the plaintiff slipped and fell a distance of about 3ft Sin and smashed his jaw. He was removed to the Infirmary where Ile was an inmate for I several weeks. He also sprained his wrist and had only been able to do light work since. After hearing the evidence I his Honour held that the plaintiff had plenty of time and Opportunity to complain of the plank. The plaintiff did not ask for a longer ladder which could then leave been placed on the floor. The plaintiff took the I risk of this plank and he (his Honour) saw no case under common law:—Mr Browne then applied under the Workmen's Compensation Act for damages.- -After some discussion as to his right to make the applica— tion, Mr Browne said the solicitor on the other side had written telling hint that the building was not 30 feet high. —Mr Tipping said he would he able to prove that the height of the building was 26 feet.—His Honour expressed the opinion that Mr Browne had no case. He was sorry for the man and had tried to find him r. case but could not.—Mr Browne said he had better withdrawthe applicatioult seemed to him there was no end to his difficulties In the matter.— His Honour agreed and the application was withdrawn, He held that Messrs Neill must pay the casts of the third party under scale B. The common law action was dismissed with I costs. Mr Tipping said Messrs Neill would take the order I for costs but would not proceed with it.

A Warrington Youth Drowned at Liverpool A young man named Arthur Hanh, liviug in Wellfield-street, Bank Qoay, Warrington, and en- gaged on his father's flat Elizabeth, which is at present at Liverpool, went to a theatre in that city on:Nonday evening with a companion and returned to Bramley-Nloore Dock late at night. On Tuesday morning he was missed, and on the water of the dock being dragged his body was recovered. How he was drowned is not yet known.

div.head: POOR CHILDREN'S TREAT
div.p: POOR CHILDREN'S TREAT

How the Little Ones Enjoyed Themselves "To make glad the hearts of many poor chil- dren during the festive season,"is,concisely stated, the aim of those ladies and gentlemen, who have for four successive years put forth strenuous efforts in order to provide the poor children of the town with an annual treat. Such an object is indeed worthy of every commendation for in Warrington there are many children, who, owing to the circumstances in which they are situated, do not often participate in the festivities which usually attend the Christmas season. To such children the treat, so thoughtfully provided by their more fortunate fellow townspeople, comes as a red letter event in their lives, and so far as one is able to judge, the I object of the promoters has been fully achieved. 4 Tharsday last week witnessed the holding of this year's treat in Parr Hall. To make adequate preparations for the treat, necessarily entails a great amount of work upon those responsible for its management, but this has been cheerfully ac- complished by a strong ladies' committee, under the presidency of the Mayoress (Mrs Parr), and with Mr Henry Taylor, Police Court Missionary, and Mr W H J Jenkins as joint secretaries. These gentlemen discharged their duties in a manner which left nothing to be desired. The treat had been eagerly looked forward to by the youngsters, and for the past week or two Mr Taylor and others connected with the committee have been besieged by applicants for tickets. The scene which the interior of Parr Hall pre- sented on Thursday evening Must have afforded pleasure to all who chanced to visit the hall. The body of the spacious building was occupied by over twelve hundred children who had taken advantage of the committee's hospitality, and the hall resounded with their shouts and merry laughter. One pleasing circumstance was noticeanle and that was that the appearance of the children as regards their dress and cleanliness was a great improvement upon last year. The arrangements on the platform were inost effective. In the foreground were four splendid Christmas trees which had been obtained by Mr Jenkins from Delamere Forest. Festoons of coloured papers had been hung across the platform and on the gallery there was a fine display of plants which had been sent from the Town Hall under the supervision of Mr. Parker, the head gardener. , Below this group of plants, there had been conven- iently arranged the toys which were to be dis- tributed to the children. As each child entered the building he or she re- ceived a package containing a meat pie, Eccles' cake and sugar bun and when all were seated at the tables the tea was served out. The tea had been supplied in barrels by Messrs Peter Walker and SOL:1 and was served under the per- sonal superintendence of Mr Monro, the manager. Needless to say the children disposed of the good things with avidity. Valuable assistance in attending to the wants of the little ones was rendered numerous workers. Tea having been partaken of, the hall was pre- pared for the entertainment. The public were allowed to watch the proceedings from the gal- leries and a large number availed themselves of the opportunity. The entertainment was furnish- ed by Messrs Archer, of Liverpool, who delighted both young and old with a lantern and cinemato- graph exhibition. At the outset photos of the Mayor and other well known townspeople were thrown on the screen and were greeted with almost deafening applause. Later in the evening the portraits of well known generals were depicted and it was remarkable to observe the quick signs of recognitiqn of these personages by the children. Still more surprising was it when a photo of Lord Itoberts was received, not with cheers but with unmistakable demonstra- tions of disapproval. The animated photos gave the youngsters the most enjoymeat, however, the display being a capital one. Most of the pictures were entirely new, that entitled "The Astro- nomer's Dream " being most novel and original. At the close of the exhibition the children marched on the platform to receive their presents and this was done in a very orderly manner. In addition to receiving a toy,each child was given an orange and a packet of sweets. About 8 o'clock the children departed for home tired, having spent a most enjoyable time, and no doubt looking forward with pleasurable anticipation to next year's treat.
THE EXAMINER FRIDAY JANUARY 17 1902

EAR LESTOWN & NEWTON 1111111111 --- E °REIGN MISSIONS AT WARGRANE. In connectiOn with the funas of the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel in foreign parts, special sermons were preached in 11 argrave Church on Sunday. The service in the morning was con- ducted by the Rev A S Cameron of the Parish Church, Warrington, and in the evening by the Rev G Vale Owen Orford, Warrington. Collections were made in aid of the society, after each service. EARLBSTOWN AND DISTRICT HOSPITAL FUND. I A meeting of the General Committee of this fund was held in the Town Hall on Tuesday evening, Dr Valentine presiding. There was a poor attendance, and but little progress was made, but hopes were held out that success would attend the project. A subscription list is in existence, but it was decided not to publish this list until something decisive had been heard from the workmen at the Viaduct Works. It was decided to hold a concert at an early date, and a demonstration during the summer.

A DISHONEST EMPLOYE. At the Liverpool Quarter Sessions on Tuesday George Thomas Dean, 25,1abourer,pleaded guilty to, at Newton, on November 27, 1901, he then being a servant to the Earlestown Industrial Co-operative Society, Limited, feloniously embezzling the sums of .C 1 and ..E1 4s lid received by him for and on account of his employers.—Mr Oulton, who prose- cuted, said prisoner was employed by the society to deliver coal, and was in a position of trust as his transactions were cash transactions.—Prisoner,who so pleaded guilty to a previous conviction, was sent to jail for four months .with hard:labour.

GOOD TEMPLARY. The Hope of Earlestown Lodge meeting was held in the Co-operative Hall, Wargrave-road on Monday evening, Bro Cutler presiding. Two candidates were initiated and one proposed. It was resolved to distribute leaflets warning parents against sending children under 14 for intoxicants. Bro Cutler read the report of the New Year social, which shewed that a pleasant evening had been spent and a fair balance left in hand. The report was sdopted with thanks to the committee. It was resolved to hold monthly Saturday evening concerts, and invite "Happy Jack" (Bro Parr) to deliver an address at the first concert. Bros Hatton and Warburton were appointed to arrange a programme for the visit to Wesley Hall Lodge, Liverpool. Bro Wood L D warned any member against accepting any invita- tion to drink port or claret wines thinking they are not intoxicating as they contained over 22 per cent of alcohol. The Lodge was closed by Bro Cutler C T in the usual manner

div.head: NOTES ON UAMES AND ATHLETICS. :RUGBY FOOTBALL.
div.p: NOTES ON UAMES AND ATHLETICS. :RUGBY FOOTBALL.
By " Ovalist."

The most inconsistent team in the League is certainly Warrington, and one needs to look no further back than over the last three results to find proof of this. On New Year's day Bradford won at Warrington by 19 points to 8 points ; on the following Saturday, War- rington took a weak team to Hull and won 15-7; while last Saturday they played practically the same team against Halifax at home, and lost 6-2. The team against Halifax was certainly the worst which War- rington has turned out this season, no less than seven of the regular players being off duty, Fish and Dicken- son through County claims, and the remainder through injuries. Still one hoped the substitutes might rise to the occasion and get two points out of Halifax, who have had a poor season. The luck was all the other way however, and seeing the weakened state of their forces Warrington required all the luck there was float- ing about.

Isherwood made a welcome re-appearance and did his best to put matters on a better footing. Ile was the best by far of the home backs and did pretty nearly all the good work that was done, and there wasn't much. Moreover, he scored the only point obtained by War- rinoton —a dropped:goal:near the close of the match.; , tr. 9

There was a very fair crowd considering all the cir- cumstances, but what enthusiasm they possessed soon evaporated. A worse game has not been seen on the Warrington ground this season—apart from " A" team matches—and the only one that runs it at all close for uninteresting features is the one with Brig- house Rangers. Neither Halifax nor Warrington played good football, passing movements being of the rarest description. There was plenty of forward play, long punting and tackling, but such a compound does not interest the spectators nowadays. The forward play on the Halifax side was uncommonly good, and the impression I formed of the Halifax eight at Hanson- large was fully confirmed. They can handle a ball as well as work the scrums and dribble, and by passing they opened the scoring on Saturday, even though the final transfer may have been forward. The home eight were inferior, though the disparity was not very appar- ent. Both the Halifax tries were scored before half- time, and the second one was fairly an eye-opener. Morley of Halifax was fairly held and had been when he parted with the ball on the line for Rig.; to walk overjwhile the Warrington men waited for the whistle. No wonder groans and hoots sounded all round the en- closure when the referee allowed the point.

Some people might blame the home players for rely- ing on the whistle, but they had ample cause. There had already been some unpleasantness and Boardman and Winskill were sent off for disagreeing while on the floor. Harris had been cautioned and generally the re- feree seemed inclined to go for the first man who showed the least unnecessary roughness. Morley got the ball out and was collared fairly and squarely. He struggled and finally got the ba 1 away, but the whistle should have gone long before. Probably if the Warrington tackler had thrown his man he would have been sent off for rough play, so the players waited for the whistle, which should certainly have sounded. Mr Marshall's decisions were very queer all afternoon and I am not surprised at the unpleasant reception the Leigh folk gave him the week before. We have had some peculiar refereeing by Yorkshire referees this season and the opinion is gaining ground that a York- shire!referee goes away with a Yorkshire team deter- mined to help Yorkshire football to a better position in the Northern League. This may sound unfair, Ibut there are plenty of people who fully believe it,as a con- sequence of the apparently biassed decisions given.

There was a Yorkshire referee when Warrington played Halifax at Halifax and a try was allowed the winners then which was never scored and which won them the match. To say the least of it Halifax at any rate have been lucky in their two engagements with Warrington this season. They have had four points out of a much better team than themselves.

Dickenson and Fish were sadly missed on Saturday and their presence might easily have turned the scale. Foster missed a certain try on the left wing which one could not conceive Fish missing, while Hockenhall was a very poor substitute for Dickenson. He has deterior- ated very much of late. The two Warrington backs do not seem to have had much chance at Barrow, as all the points and glory were scooped up by the Brough- tonians. They would have been far more use at Wilderspool. Allen and R Bate both played poorly behind the scrum and missed many chances of opening out the game. Ratcliffe was good at full back and Harris fair, though he suffered through the stupid way in which the halves played on the opposite and inferior wing. They only gave Isherwood and Harris about half the passes that the other couple got and the result was failure. On the Halifax side, Morley and Little were the best men, though the full back was not so good as he was on the occasion of the previous meet- ing of Halifax and Warrington.

Warrington would have been third instead of seventh had they won on Saturday. The leaders easily accoun- ted for Leigh even with Eve men off, and Oldham and Swinton obtained easy victories at the expense of Hunslet and Brighouse Rangers.

Last week I suggested that Warrington might lose against Halifax, and as they conclusively proved their inconsistency there is good reason why I should venture on a prophecy that they will win at Swinton to-day. At any rate they will be fully represented once more, the lame, the sick, and the County players all being expected to turn out. One or two forward changes have been made, and G Jolley a 13 stone man from Fletcher's defunct team,is given a trial along with his brother. The fifteen will be as follows. Hallam, full back ; Fish, Isherwood, Dickenson and Harris, three-quarters ; Burgess and Allen, half-backs ; Board- man, Taylor,.Morrison, J Swift, W Swift, J Jolley, G Jolley and Edmondson forwards.

Swinton will also place their best team in the field, the picked side being as follows.—A Chorley, back ; V R Hampson, "Bob"- Valentine (captain), W Wall- work, and J H Cooper, three-quarters ; " Dai "Davies and F A Morgan, half-backs ; H Barnett, .1 Evans, J Preston, E Yates, C Pollitt, T Pomfret, R Tickle, and J Blackburn, forwards. Reserve, E Vigors.

Of recent years Swinton have had the best of their engagements with Warrington and besides winning at home have taken points from Wilderspool on the last three occasions. Previously each team won with al- most unfailing regularity on its own enclosure' though Warrington did once get the better of the Blues at Swinton when Barber was at his best. Swinton have been lucky in their wins at Warrington and if a bit of their luck stays with Warrington to-day the order of things may be changed. Anyhow it should be a rattling good game.

Swinton " A " have designs on the Combination championship, and the team to visit Warrington on Saturday is the most powerful turned out this season. "Jack "Lewis partners Messer on the right wing, and in addition to these two players the others on the side who may be regarded as first teamers are J Jones, " Dick Jones, Cheetham, Harris, and Berry. This , ,cviii he Lewis' first turn out since his injury against Hunslet on November 2. Warrington "A" will also be strongly represented and a big effort will be made to upset the pretensions of Jun Valentine and his men. The stay-at•homes should likewise witness an interest- ing struggle.

The " A " team made a very poor show at Rochdale and most of the blame is attached to the regular play- ers, who displayed miserable form. Brown, Clare and Jolley of Fletcher s team all made a promising debut and are given further trial.

'Though they do not figure prominently in the reports I hear that both Fish and Dickenson played very well at Barrow and quite pleased the county officials. Valentine may possibly get the centre .position against Yorkshire but Fish seems pretty certain to be the left wing man.
Runcorn defeated Wigan at Irwell-lane by 8 points to 5 points on Saturday in the South-West Lancashire Competition..

div.head: REV. C. F. AKED AT NEWTON.
div.p: THE REV. C. F. AKED AT NEWTON.

Under the auspices of the Newton-le-Willows Mutua' Imprevement Society, a lecture was given in the Con- gregational Schoolroom, Newton, on Monday evening, the subject being" The coming of the people." Owing to the incident at Liverpool, in which Mr Abed was the central figure, sinister rumours were floated in Earles- town, but upon what grounds could not very well be ascertained. Notwithstanding r the disclaimer by Mr Allatt,that thellecture would have no reference to:tlie War a good number of people wended their way to the Con- gregational School, and congregated outside in Crow lane, but there was no disturbance, nor even a sembl- ance of one, and the lecture proceeded witheut hindrance. There was a good company inside the room over which the Rev James Allatt presided. The Chairman said the Newton-le-Willows Mutual Improvement Society was a very mixed company. They were drawn from the four winds of heaven. Although they were such as he had described, the armest of the supporters, and the bitterest enemies of Dr Ahed heartily congratulated him upon his entire escape from serious physical injury. What things were possible in Liverpool were entirely impossible in an enlightened district like Newton. (Hear, hear.) The Lecturer said they were living faster than ever man lived before. If they said of the past year that it was the most crowded and eventful in their memory, what should they say of the century. Going back to I the 16th Century he showed the condition of things as regarded the government of the country. The 19th Century was described as that whieh had seen the coming of the people, the transfer of political power from the privileged few to the great masses of the people, the century of the making of democracy. If they were going to understand the 19th century they would have to begin at the 18th. At the beginning of 19th century a representative Government in this country scarcely existed at all. There was little of it, and what there was was bad ,almost rotten. 70 members of the House of Commons were elected by 35 members of the House of Lords, the Duke of Rutland owned 13, the Duke of Norfolk 7, and generally the controlling factor was the great landlords. Boroughs were bought and sold and the price was known beforehand and the theory was that there need not be any representation at all. It was held seriously that the British people had no tight to self Government at all. The King ruled by divine right. Things were worse in Scotland, for all tbe county voters in the whole of Scotland numbered 2,000, but in the County of Bute which returned a member of Parliament, there was only one voter: There was nct a voter in all the towns and boroughs of Scotland, for the City COUNICiI9 elected a committee which made its selection and sent its member to the House cf Commons. The beginning of the 19th Century was a time of terrible suffering. The hideous Factory System had come into existence; female labour in the mines. He alluded to the cern laws .and the bread riots. Then the people began to have an idea that the Government of the conntry had some- thing to do with the state of the country,and it dawned upon their minds that they were being badly gOyerned• Shelley called to the people to arise. William ' Cobbett taught the people that they were being badly governed, and he told them they would never get rid of this until the Government of the country was chanted, and they must get hold of the vote. Referring to the Reform Bill of 1832, this bill, he said, laid once and for ever, that ghost of superstitien that there was no right of representation in the British people. It let the middle classes into power, it shoulder- ed out in the cold the working classes, and laid the foundation of political emancipation and political ee- franchisement. There sprang up among the workine classes a burning desire for the franchise, for eceitical liberty. He referred to the Chartist movement and said as years went on they ;found they I came soon to the enfranchisement of tlie• people ; first in the Boroughs, admitting at last the working man to power. Alen with all this was the reception of the ballot hex. With this they would see in part, in this country the coming of the people. What was necessary, he asked, to complete the making of democracy in our own country. He knew that they represented no political party there that night. He did not ,belong to any political party. He was not going to tell them what they ought to do to complete the coming of the democracy. They might say the working man had already got a good deal too much power, and he did not want to give him any more. If they wanted to complete the coming of the democracy, they had got to abolish the hereditary member in the House of Lords. From the point of view of democracy a hereditary legis- lator was just as silly as a hereditary mathematician. They would have to arrange for one man one vote, and one vote 6ne value. Until they could arrange for the abolition of canvassing they would never get a pure represeotaticn. Arrange for the payment of members of Parliament. They would never get their Own opinions spoken by their own member until there was payment of members. They were bound to choose inside a certain circle from min who had money and who could afford to live in London. Nothing could ever make it right for the destinies of millions of people to depend upon the accident of a man's birth because that man was the son of his father, because be had done the world the honour of getting himself born. Was it not well that we should be free, apart from the result of our freedom. Carlisle said our boasted liberty was only a liberty to go wrong. It was better to have the liberty to go wrong than not to have the liberty at all. It was better for us to be free that we should have a chance to move our limbs and let our minds; expand and work our own salvation socially and politically though it be in fear and trembling. What had democracy done ? Had it been for good ? Nothing could make it right that they should be bound and not be free. What had democracy done P He named one thing, education. He begged them to watch the movement asiainst education in this country—because there was a conspiracy to put back education, to crush, dwarf, binder, if possible to destroy the education of the people for a purpose and that purpose was to put back democracy. They did not believe in education because they did not believe in democracy, because they knew an educated democracy would make short work of them. (Applause.)

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD, The First Meeting of the New Board.
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD, The First Meeting of the New Board.
Oa_ Tuesday. _evening the first meeting of the new

was field in the. Board room. The.re was a full attendance of members, Mr R H Posnett for the first time taking the place of Mr Cunningham. rhe Board room with its clerk, Mr Lightburn ; the assistant clerk, Mr A Lightburn; and the four pressmen,presented quite an animated appearance and on the election of Mr F J Norman, to the chair pro tern, the happy family settled down to business with quite a pleasant and good hnmoured air.
Board
ELECTION OF CHAIRMAN.

The first business of the Board 4w; the election of chairman for the ensuing three years. It will be remembered that during the last campaign Canon Wood predicted that if the Progressives won they would certainly put in power a progressive chair- man. For once at all events, the Vicar prophesied ' alight. In a neat concise speech Mr F J Norman pro- posed that Mr Pritchard be elected chairman of the Board. They all knew, he said, that Mr James Pritchard had been a member of the Bard for twenty seven years—in fact since its establishment. For a long time he had occupied an honourable position as chairman of the Board, and he hoped they would be perfectly unanimous in electing him once again to the chair. There were stirring times before them and they would all endorse the opinion that, with the wealth of his past experience on educational matters, he would be invaluable to them as a Board.

In seconding the motion, Mr Taylor remarked that they would all be pleased to see Mr Pritchard once more in a position to which he had done honour for so long. There was no amendment frnm the "ratepayers' candidates," so the resolution was declared duly carried after the usual show of hands.
Mr Norman then vacated the chair,taking his custom- ary position at the end of the table opposite the chair, while Mr Pritchard took the seat compulsorily vacated by him three years agn.
THE CHAIRMAN'. ADDRESS TO THE BOARD._

In accepting the honour conferred upon him Mr Pritchard delivered a weighty speech in which he I briefly indicated what 'would be the future policy of the Progressive party. After thanking them, he said that if he bad consulted his own feelings he would have remained a private member, but after the unanimous vote of his colleagues he could do no other than comply. He felt he could rely on the forbearance and co-opera- tion of all. It was not likely that in the future they would be called upon to provide further school accommodation. It would be their duty to maintain the efficiency of the Board Schools and to secure the attendance of all children of school age. They were informed by Cabinet minis- tars that an important Education Bill would be intro- duced in Parliament at an early date which would have _ _

, far reaching effect. It would be their duty to closely consider that Bill. If in their opinion it was favourable to public elementary education they would welcome it, but, if it were hostile they would protest against it. Rumour said that School Boards might be threatened, and there were many advocates for one authority to deal with elementary and secondary education. If it were possible to create a superior authority than the Board there would be no reason to complain. He had taken part in every School Board contest in Runcorn. During the last election he was impressed by the enthusiasm manifested towards the School Board and Board schools. There was a day when this was not so. They were now coming into popular favour, and the ratepayers were interested intelligently in their work. They were proud of their schools and were cheerfully prepared to bear a small burden on the rates This could be attributed to the children attending the Board schools, for the parents saw for themselves the sanitary condition of the 'ratepayers' schools and the healthy condition under which their children were taught. The Board school was the beginning of a national system of education which should he universal. (Applause).
A PROGRESSIVE VICE CHAIRMAN.

" The next matter," the Chairman continued after a slight pause "is the election of a vice chairman." There was a speedy response from Mr Handley, who proposed Mr Taylor. " I do not think," said he," that I need do more than mention his name to) secure the un- animous consent offeverybody." Mr Norman, in seconding, remarked that Mr Taylor had rendered yeoman service in educational work and he would be delighted to see him in the position of vice chairman.—Tbere was again no amendment, and the propositioa was passed.
THE COMSEITTEES,
It was resolved that the School Management Com- mitt•:e and the School Attendance Commitcee consist of the members of the whole Board on the proposition of Mr Handley.

THE FINANCE COMMITTEE, In considering the composition of the Finance Com- mittee the chairman remarked that it was composed of three members and asked for nominations. Mr Norman pointed out that the committee was created three years ago.falt would be wise to revert to the old system when the finance was merged into the work of the School Management Committee. Mr Imison disagreed with Mr Norman but after a little discussion it was resolved that the finances of the Board form the work in future of the School Manage- ment Committee.

div.head: DATE OF MEETINGS ALTERED.
div.p: DATE OF MEETINGS ALTERED.

A very useful alteration was made with respect to the holding of the Board meeting each month. Mr Norman showed how inconvenienced the press were through the Board meetings being held late on Thursday evening and thought it would be better if they could be held at 5.30. p.m. on the last Tuesday in each month. This proving favourable to all Canon Wood seconded the resolution which was carried. This concluded the whole of the business.

div.head: Captain G R Crosfield and the Boer War.
div.p: Captain G R Crosfield and the Boer War.

Captain G R Crosfield gave a very interesting lecture 1 before the members of the Workingmen's Mission Mutual Improvement Class on Tuesday evening, in which he dealt with the history of the Boers in South Africa. The lecture was delivered in the schoolroom, Thewlis-street, before a large attendance. Mr Williams presided and briefly introduced the lecturer. Captain Crosfield said he did not intend to deal with the subject from a party standpoint, his facts were based upon the 1 official blue books. At the outset he referred to the settlement of the Dutch at the Cape in 1652 and proceeded to trace their history lin South Africa from that date t) the present. The great trek acrossthe Vaal was alluded to and Captain Crosfield, in dealing with their disputes with the British, quoted at length from the despatches during the complicated negotiations which preceded the present war. Be also read passages from Dr A Conan Doyle's book " The Great Boer War" and com- mended the book to the consideration of his audience. The progress of the present war was briefly traced,Cap- tain Crosfield pointed out that the strategical position of the Boers was a very strong one and under good leadership the There might have reached the coast before the British could stop them. Instead of that they wasted much energy and employed a large number of men to attack a little place like Mafeking. In alluding to the military aspects of the war, he said it had aroused greater interest in the army, and especially in the volunteer forces. The volunteers had come out well in this war and he wished to put in a very strong. plea to able-bodied young men to serve their country by joining the Volunteer force.—A discussion followed, and at the close Captain Crosfield's services were heartily acknowledged.
Animated Pictures at Parr Hall.

It is seldom that Warrington people have the opportunity of witnessing a more unique and high- ly interesting entertainment than that which has .been presented at Parr Hall every evening this week by the Thomas—Edison Animated Photo Company. The remarkable development of animated photography has been one of the wonders of recent years and probably the collection possessed by the Thomas—Edison Company is unexcelled in this country. Up-to-dateness is the distinguish- ing feature for by means of the company's instru- ment, the historiagraph, passing events of national and local interest are vividly depicted. As an instance of the enterprise of the company in this direction it may be mentioned that in Parr Hall this wesk scenes representing the home com- ing of the Prince and Princess of Wales after their tour _round the world have been exhibited and there is alsol a series of pictures illustrative of dramatic episodes in the Boer war. A still more striking photograph, locally, is that which repro- duces phases of the football match last Saturday between Warrington and Halifax. The picture is a remarkably clear one and many interesting incidents are portrayed including the sending off the field of two players, A splendid series of pic- tures is that representing the life and death of Joan of Arc whilet other photographs thrown on the screen depict scenes of a laughable and mysti- fying description. The master-piece however, is tte animated Christmas pantomime " Blue Beard" which is presented in twelve scenes and surpasses anything of its kind which has ever been produced in Warrington. The pictures are all lif e- size and are absolutely free from flickering. Fresh novelties are introduced at every entertainment and altogether, the programme is one of unusual excellence. A pleasing diversion is supplied in the form of a ventriloquial sketch by Mr J W Delmar. The visit of the company will extend over another week, and matinees will be given on Saturdays and I Wednesday.

The Liverpool Diocesan Lay Readers.'i,":q At the special invitation of the Bishop, the Hon. Licensed Lay Readers of the diocese met at the palace on Monday evening and were received by his Lordship and Mrs Chavasse. Tea and coffee were served from 4.30 to 6 30, after which a short special service was held in St. Saviour's Church, Faulkner-square. The Bishop delivered an address emphasizing three special points for his hearers' attention, viz., that they should be right (I) with God; (2) with themselves; and (3) with the people to whom they were'privileged to minister. Amongst those present from various parts of the diocese were Mr H J Westbrook (Holy Trinity, Warrington) and Dr Mounc.ey (St Johns, Rarlestown).
